98417.e: The saddle is the seat of the bike. It should be high enough for your legs to be almost straight when you pedal.
98417.m: When cycling you sit on the saddle.

98418.q: What do you steer a bike with?
98418.e: With the handlebars you turn the front wheel left or right. That is how you choose your direction.

98419.q: Where at the back of a bike can you fix a bag?
98419.e: The pannier rack sits at the back above the rear wheel. You can fix bags or a basket to it.
98419.m: You carry bags on the pannier rack.

98420.q: Why does a moving bike not fall over as easily as one standing still?
98420.e: A moving bike is easy to keep balanced. Small steering movements stop it from tipping over.
98420.m: A moving bike stays balanced more easily.

98421.q: From what age may children in Switzerland ride a bike alone on a main road?
98421.e: In Switzerland children from the age of 6 may ride alone on main roads. Younger children need someone with them who is at least 16.
98421.m: You may ride alone on a main road from age 6.

98422.q: In Switzerland, must every bike have a bell?
98422.e: In Switzerland every bike must have a bell. You can use it to warn others.
98422.m: A bike bell is compulsory in Switzerland.

98423.q: Up to what age may children in Switzerland cycle on the pavement if there is no cycle path?
98423.e: Children may ride on the pavement until their 12th birthday if there is no cycle path or cycle lane. They must look out for pedestrians.
98423.m: Children up to 12 may cycle carefully on the pavement.

98424.q: A bike has 2 chainrings at the front and 10 sprockets at the back. How many gears does it have?
98424.e: Each of the 2 chainrings works with each of the 10 sprockets. 2 times 10 makes 20 gears.
98424.m: Count the gears as chainrings times sprockets.

98425.q: Where are the brake levers on most bikes?
98425.e: The brake levers are on the handlebars. So you can brake with your hands without letting go.
98425.m: The brake levers are on the handlebars.

98426.q: How do you brake with a coaster brake?
a: You put your feet on the ground
98426.e: With a coaster brake you push the pedals backwards. Then the rear wheel brakes.
98426.m: With a coaster brake you pedal backwards.

98427.q: What is produced at the brakes when you brake?
98427.e: When you brake, the brake pads rub. The friction makes the brakes warm.

98428.q: When is a bike's braking distance longer?
98428.e: On wet roads and with wet brakes, everything grips less well. That is why it takes longer to stop.
98428.m: In the wet a bike takes longer to stop.

98429.q: Which bike brake presses brake blocks against the edge of the wheel?
98429.e: The rim brake presses two brake blocks against the rim, the edge of the wheel.
98429.m: The rim brake brakes on the edge of the wheel.

98430.q: Which bike brake has a metal disc in the middle of the wheel?
98430.e: With a disc brake, a metal disc is fixed to the wheel hub. Brake pads grip this disc.
98430.m: The disc brake brakes on a metal disc.

98431.q: What is the safest way to brake?
a: With both brakes at the same time
Only with the front brake, very hard
With your feet on the ground
98431.e: Using both brakes together is the safest way to stop. Braking very hard with only the front brake can send you over the handlebars.
98431.m: The safest way to brake is with both brakes.

98432.q: Why does a bike have gears?
a: So that you can ride more easily or faster
So that the light comes on
So that the bell is louder
So that the saddle goes higher
98432.e: With gears you adjust how hard you pedal. Uphill you choose a low gear, on flat ground a high gear.
98432.m: Gears let you adjust the effort of pedalling.

98433.q: Which gear do you choose when the road goes steeply uphill?
98433.e: In a low gear the pedals are easy to turn. That way you can manage steep stretches too.
98433.m: Uphill you ride in a low gear.

98434.q: What are the small cogs on the rear wheel called?
98434.e: There are several cogs on the rear wheel, the sprockets. The chain runs over one of them.
98434.m: The cogs on the rear wheel are called sprockets.

98435.q: With which kind of gears can you see several cogs side by side on the rear wheel?
98435.e: With derailleur gears, a mechanism pushes the chain onto a different cog. With hub gears, the gears are hidden inside the hub.
98435.m: Derailleur gears move the chain from cog to cog.

98436.q: Where are the gears hidden with hub gears?
a: In the middle of the rear wheel
98436.e: With hub gears, the gears are built into the hub, that is, the middle of the rear wheel.
98436.m: With hub gears, the gears are hidden in the rear wheel.

98437.q: What do you have to do when changing gear with derailleur gears?
98437.e: The chain can only change when it is moving. So you have to keep pedalling while changing gear, but without much force.
98437.m: With derailleur gears you keep pedalling while changing.

98438.q: What is a high gear good for?
98438.e: In a high gear you go a long way with each turn of the pedals. That is good for riding fast on flat stretches.
98438.m: On flat ground you ride fast in a high gear.

98439.q: Where is the gear lever on most bikes?
98439.e: The gear levers are on the handlebars. So you can change gear while riding.
98439.m: The gear lever is on the handlebars.

98440.q: What does the chain do on a bike?
a: It takes the power to the rear wheel
It holds the saddle in place
98440.e: The chain connects the front cog with the rear wheel. That way the power of your legs drives the rear wheel.
98440.m: The chain takes the power of your legs to the rear wheel.

98441.q: What is a bike chain made of?
98441.e: A bike chain is made of many small steel links. They are joined together so they can move.
98441.m: A bike chain is made of many metal links.

98442.q: What does a bike chain need to run well?
98442.e: Chain oil lubricates the links. That way the chain runs quietly and rusts less.

98443.q: What happens to a chain that often gets wet and is never looked after?
98443.e: Steel rusts when it gets wet. Looking after it with oil protects the chain.

98444.q: What is a chain guard on a bike good for?
98444.e: The chain guard covers the chain. That way your trousers and fingers stay clean and do not get caught in the chain.
98444.m: The chain guard protects trousers and fingers.

98445.q: What does the bike chain run over at the front, by the pedals?
98445.e: At the front, on the crank, there is a large cog, the chainring. The chain fits into its teeth.
98445.m: At the front the chain runs over the chainring.

98446.q: What can happen if the chain is loose?
98446.e: A loose or badly adjusted chain can jump off the cog. Then you cannot pedal the bike forward any more.
98446.m: A loose chain can come off.

98447.q: What fits into the gaps in the chain?
98447.e: The teeth of the cogs fit exactly into the gaps in the chain. That way it does not slip.
98447.m: The teeth of the cogs fit into the chain.

98448.q: What do you use to push the pedals?
98448.e: Your feet rest on the pedals and push them round in a circle.
98448.m: You push the pedals with your feet.

98449.q: What movement do the pedals make when you ride?
a: They go round in a circle
98449.e: The pedals are attached to the cranks. When you pedal, they go round in a circle.
98449.m: The pedals go round in a circle.

98450.q: What colour are the reflectors on the pedals in Switzerland?
98450.e: Pedal reflectors are orange or yellow. They move as you pedal, so they stand out well in headlights.
98450.m: Pedal reflectors are orange or yellow.

98451.q: What are the arms the pedals are attached to called?
98451.e: The cranks connect the pedals to the chainring. They work like levers.
98451.m: The pedals are attached to the cranks.

98452.q: Why do people sometimes stand up on the pedals when going uphill?
a: To push with their body weight
98452.e: When you stand, your own body weight presses on the pedals. That way you can put in more force.
98452.m: Standing up, your body weight presses hard on the pedals.

98453.q: Which part of your foot is best for pushing the pedal?
98453.e: With the ball of your foot on the pedal you can pass on the most force.
98453.m: Pedal with the ball of your foot.

98454.q: What is special about clipless pedals?
a: The shoe clicks into the pedal
98454.e: With clipless pedals, a plate on the shoe clicks into the pedal. That way your foot does not slip off.
98454.m: With clipless pedals the shoe clicks in.

98455.q: How many pedals does a normal bike have?
98455.e: A bike has one pedal for the left foot and one for the right.

98456.q: What colour is the rear light on a bike?
98456.e: The light at the back of a bike is red. Cars have red rear lights too.
98456.m: A bike's rear light is red.

98457.q: When must you switch on your bike lights in Switzerland?
a: At night and when visibility is poor
98457.e: At night, in tunnels and when visibility is poor, bikes must have lights at the front and back.
98457.m: At night and in poor visibility a bike needs lights.

98458.q: Why do you need lights on your bike at dusk?
a: So that the bike gets warmer
98458.e: With lights, drivers and pedestrians see you much sooner. You can also see the way better yourself.

98459.q: Where in Switzerland must you ride with lights on even during the day?
98459.e: It is dark in a tunnel. That is why you need bike lights there even during the day.
98459.m: In a tunnel a bike always needs lights.

98460.q: Where does a bike light without a dynamo get its electricity from?
a: From a battery or rechargeable battery
From the air in the tyre
98460.e: Many bike lights have a battery or a rechargeable battery. You charge the rechargeable battery at a socket.
98460.m: Bike lights without a dynamo need a battery.

98461.q: What must you do if a bike light with a rechargeable battery stops working?
98461.e: A flat battery gives no more electricity. After charging, the light works again.
98461.m: A flat battery must be charged again.

98462.q: Which kind of light on bikes is bright and saves energy?
98462.e: LED lights are very bright and use little electricity. That is why almost all bike lights have LEDs today.
98462.m: LED lights are bright and save energy.

98463.q: What do you have to do with a bottle dynamo to make the light come on?
98463.e: A bottle dynamo only works when its little wheel is touching the tyre. So to switch it on, you flip it against the tyre.
98463.m: You flip a bottle dynamo against the tyre.

98464.q: When does a light with a simple dynamo shine?
a: When the bike is standing still
98464.e: The dynamo only makes electricity while the wheel is turning. When the bike stops, a simple dynamo light goes out.
98464.m: A dynamo only makes electricity when the wheel turns.

a: In the middle of the front wheel
98465.e: The hub dynamo is built into the hub of the front wheel, that is, the middle of the wheel.
98465.m: The hub dynamo sits in the middle of the front wheel.

98466.q: What does a bottle dynamo rub against?
98466.e: A small wheel on the bottle dynamo presses against the side of the tyre. When the tyre turns, the little wheel turns too.
98466.m: The bottle dynamo turns along with the tyre.

98467.q: What is inside a dynamo and helps to make electricity?
98467.e: Inside the dynamo, a magnet turns next to a coil of wire. This produces electricity.
98467.m: In a dynamo a turning magnet makes electricity.

98468.q: What do you often notice when pedalling with the dynamo switched on?
98468.e: To make electricity, the dynamo needs some force. This force comes from your legs.
98468.m: The dynamo's electricity takes a bit of leg power.

98469.q: What does the standlight on a bike with a dynamo do?
a: It keeps shining when you stop
It only shines when it rains
It goes off when you brake
98469.e: A standlight stores a little electricity. So the lamp keeps shining for a while when you wait at the traffic lights.
98469.m: A standlight keeps shining when you stop.

98470.q: Does a light with a dynamo need a battery?
a: Yes, but only at the back
98470.e: The dynamo makes the electricity itself as long as you are riding. That is why you do not need a battery.
98470.m: A dynamo light needs no battery.

98471.q: Where are the stabilisers on a child's bike?
a: On the left and right of the rear wheel
At the front on the handlebars
On top of the front wheel
98471.e: The two small stabiliser wheels are fixed on the left and right of the rear wheel.
98471.m: Stabilisers are next to the rear wheel.

a: To stop the bike from tipping over
98472.e: Stabilisers keep the bike upright. That way it does not tip to the side even when standing still.
98472.m: Stabilisers stop the bike tipping over.

98473.q: What do you hardly learn with stabilisers?
98473.e: With stabilisers you do not have to balance. That is why you hardly learn balance with them.
98473.m: With stabilisers you hardly learn to balance.

98474.q: What do many children use today instead of stabilisers to learn balance?
98474.e: On a balance bike you push off with your feet and balance at the same time. That is how you learn balance.
98474.m: On a balance bike you learn to balance.

98475.q: What can happen in a fast bend with stabilisers?
98475.e: With stabilisers you cannot lean into the bend. At high speed the bike therefore easily tips outwards.
98475.m: Bikes with stabilisers can tip over in fast bends.

98476.q: How many stabilisers does a child's bike usually have?
98476.e: A child's bike usually has two stabilisers, one on each side.
98476.m: A child's bike usually has two stabilisers.

98477.q: When do you take the stabilisers off?
98477.e: Once the child can keep their balance alone, they no longer need stabilisers.
98477.m: If you can balance, you no longer need stabilisers.

98478.q: A bike has two wheels and two stabilisers. How many wheels is that altogether?
98478.e: The front wheel and back wheel are 2 wheels. Then there are 2 stabilisers. 2 plus 2 makes 4.
98478.m: Two wheels and two stabilisers make four wheels.

98479.q: What do you pump into a bike tyre?
98479.e: Inside the tyre is an inner tube full of air. The air makes the tyre firm and springy.
98479.m: You pump air into a bike tyre.

98480.q: What do you use to pump up a bike tyre?
98480.e: With a bike pump you push air through the valve into the inner tube.
98480.m: A bike pump puts air into the tyre.

98481.q: Through which part does the air get into the inner tube?
98481.e: The valve lets air in but not back out. That way the tyre stays firm.
98481.m: Air gets into the inner tube through the valve.

98482.q: In which unit is tyre pressure often measured?
98482.e: The pressure in a tyre is often given in bar. The right number is usually printed on the tyre.
98482.m: Tyre pressure is measured in bar.

98483.q: What is it like riding a bike with too little air in the tyres?
98483.e: A soft tyre squashes a lot. It rolls less well, and you have to pedal harder.
98483.m: With too little air, a bike is hard work to ride.

98484.q: What happens if an inner tube has a hole?
98484.e: Air streams out through a hole. The tyre goes flat and you have a ‘puncture’.
98484.m: If there is a hole, the air escapes from the tyre.

98485.q: Who built an air-filled tyre for his son's tricycle in 1887 and made it well known?
98485.e: John Boyd Dunlop built an air-filled tyre for his son's tricycle in 1887 and patented it in 1888. It made the ride much smoother.
98485.m: Dunlop made the air-filled tyre well known.

98486.q: How do you find a small hole in an inner tube?
a: You put it in the sun
98486.e: In water, air bubbles rise where the hole is. That way you can see it exactly.
98486.m: In water, bubbles give the hole away.

98487.q: How should a bike helmet sit?
a: Straight and firm on your head
Loose at the back of your neck
98487.e: A helmet only protects you if it sits straight on your head and covers your forehead. It must not wobble.
98487.m: A helmet sits straight and firm on your head.

98488.q: What holds a bike helmet in place under your chin?
98488.e: The chin strap is fastened under your chin. That way the helmet stays on your head if you fall.
98488.m: The chin strap holds the helmet in place.

98489.q: What should you do with your helmet after a bad fall?
a: Wash it and keep wearing it
98489.e: In a fall, the foam inside the helmet can be damaged, even if you cannot see it. That is why you need a new helmet afterwards.
98489.m: After a bad fall you need a new helmet.

98490.q: Is a bike helmet compulsory in Switzerland for normal bikes?
98490.e: For normal bikes there is no helmet requirement in Switzerland (as of 2025). But experts strongly recommend wearing one.
98490.m: A bike helmet is not compulsory, but strongly recommended.

98491.q: What is inside a bike helmet that absorbs the impact?
98491.e: There is hard foam inside the helmet. It is squashed in an impact and so protects your head.
98491.m: The foam in a helmet absorbs the impact.

98492.q: Why does a bike helmet have holes?
a: So that air cools your head
So that it breaks more easily
So that you can hear better
98492.e: Air flows through the vents. That way you sweat less under the helmet.
98492.m: The holes in a helmet let air through.

98493.q: Which helmet colour is especially easy to see in traffic?
98493.e: Light, bright colours stand out well in traffic. Dark helmets are harder to see.
98493.m: A bright helmet is easy to see.

98494.q: What is another name for a bike reflector?
98494.e: Reflectors are also called cat's eyes. Cats' eyes also light up in the dark when light shines into them.
98494.m: A reflector is also called a cat's eye.

98495.q: Does a reflector light up by itself?
98495.e: A reflector has no lamp. It sends back the light that falls on it, for example from a car.
98495.m: A reflector sends back light from elsewhere.

98496.q: What colour is the reflector at the back of a bike?
98496.e: There must be a red reflector at the back of a bike. It matches the colour of the rear light.
98496.m: The reflector at the back of a bike is red.

98497.q: What colour is the reflector at the front of a bike?
98497.e: There must be a white reflector at the front of a bike. That way people can tell which is the front.
98497.m: The reflector at the front of a bike is white.

98498.q: In which direction does a reflector send the light?
98498.e: A reflector sends the light back to where it came from. That way the driver behind the headlights can see it well.
98498.m: A reflector sends light back towards the lamp.

98499.q: When can you see a reflector best?
a: In total darkness with no light
98499.e: A reflector needs light from outside. Without light it stays dark.
98499.m: A reflector needs light to shine.

98500.q: What do you wear in the dark so that you are seen better on foot or on a bike?
98500.e: Reflectors on clothes send back the light from cars. That way you are seen much sooner.
98500.m: Reflectors on your clothes make you visible.

98501.q: Where does the cat's eye on a bike get its name from?
a: It shines in the light like a cat's eyes
It is as small as a cat's eye
It is green like a cat's eye
It is round like a cat's eye
98501.e: Cats have a layer behind the retina that reflects light. That is why their eyes shine in headlights, just like a reflector.
98501.m: Cats' eyes shine in the light like reflectors.

98502.q: What do you call a road that goes over a high mountain, like the Gotthard?
98502.e: A pass is a road over a mountain crossing. On a bike it goes steeply uphill for a long way.

98503.q: What happens going downhill if you do not pedal?
98503.e: Downhill, gravity pulls the bike down. It rolls faster and faster, so you have to brake.
98503.m: Downhill a bike speeds up by itself.

98504.q: What can you do if a hill is too steep to ride up?
a: Get off and push the bike
Let the air out of the tyres
98504.e: If it is too steep, you get off and push. That is completely normal and safe.
98504.m: If it is too steep, push the bike.

98505.q: What helps on an e-bike going uphill?
98505.e: On an e-bike, an electric motor helps you pedal. That way you get up the hill more easily.
98505.m: On an e-bike a motor helps you pedal.

98506.q: What is especially important when riding a bike downhill?
98506.e: Downhill you go fast. You must brake early and with both brakes so that you do not go too fast.

98507.q: What is the easiest way to pedal uphill?
98507.e: Steady, calm pedalling saves energy. If you pedal jerkily, you get tired more quickly.

98508.q: Who finds it easier to ride a bike up a hill?
98508.e: The less weight you have to take uphill, the less effort you need.
98508.m: Less weight makes riding uphill easier.

98509.q: Where in Switzerland do you often have to cycle uphill?
a: Along the shore of Lake Constance
98509.e: The Alps have many steep roads and passes. There you often go uphill for a long way.
98509.m: In the Alps you often cycle uphill.

98610.q: In which unit is radiative forcing given?
98610.e: Radiative forcing is an energy flux density. It states how many watts per square metre of the Earth's surface are added to or missing from the climate system.
98610.m: Radiative forcing is measured in watts per square metre.

98611.q: What does the radiative forcing of a factor such as CO2 or aerosol describe?
a: The change in the Earth's radiation balance caused by this factor
The speed at which wind distributes heat
The amount of sunlight plants store
The temperature in the Earth's core
98611.e: A positive forcing means that more energy comes in than goes out, which warms the Earth. A negative forcing has a cooling effect.
98611.m: A positive radiative forcing adds extra energy to the climate system.

98612.q: According to the formula ΔF = 5.35 · ln(C/C0), what radiative forcing does a doubling of the CO2 content produce?
98612.e: With a doubling, C/C0 = 2 and ln 2 ≈ 0.693. 5.35 · 0.693 gives about 3.7 W/m².
98612.m: A doubling of CO2 corresponds to a forcing of just under 4 watts per square metre.

98613.q: According to ΔF = 5.35 · ln(C/C0), what radiative forcing does a rise in CO2 from 280 to 420 ppm produce?
98613.e: The ratio is 420/280 = 1.5 and ln 1.5 ≈ 0.405. 5.35 · 0.405 gives about 2.2 W/m².
98613.m: Even an increase of half in CO2 produces a clear forcing.

98614.q: Why does an increase from 280 to 560 ppm CO2 cause about the same forcing as one from 560 to 1120 ppm?
a: Forcing grows with the square of the concentration
Above 560 ppm CO2 no longer has any effect
The ocean always takes up exactly half
98614.e: The most important absorption bands are already saturated in their centre; the effect only keeps growing at the edges. That is why the ratio counts, not the difference in concentrations.
98614.m: For CO2 forcing, every doubling counts the same.

98615.q: Overall, what sign does the radiative forcing of human-made aerosols have?
a: Negative, they have a cooling effect
Positive, they have a strong warming effect
98615.e: Suspended particles such as sulphate scatter sunlight back into space and make clouds brighter. In this way they mask part of the warming caused by greenhouse gases.
98615.m: Air pollution by aerosols temporarily slows warming.

98616.q: According to the sixth IPCC report, roughly how large was the total human-caused effective radiative forcing in 2019 compared with 1750?
98616.e: The IPCC gives a best estimate of 2.72 W/m². This combines warming greenhouse gases and cooling aerosols.
98616.m: Humans have shifted the Earth's energy balance by almost 3 watts per square metre.

98617.q: After the eruption of Pinatubo in 1991, by roughly how much did the global average temperature temporarily fall?
98617.e: The volcano threw sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere, where sulphate droplets formed. These reflected sunlight and cooled the Earth for about one to two years.
98617.m: Large volcanic eruptions cause a short negative radiative forcing.

98618.q: What best estimate does the sixth IPCC report give for equilibrium climate sensitivity?
98618.e: For a doubling of the CO2 content, the IPCC expects long-term warming of 3 °C as the best value. It bases this on several independent lines of evidence.
98618.m: In the long term, a doubling of CO2 warms the Earth by about 3 °C.

98619.q: What likely range does the sixth IPCC report give for equilibrium climate sensitivity?
98619.e: The IPCC was able to reduce the uncertainty considerably compared with earlier reports. Values below 1.5 °C are now considered extremely unlikely.
98619.m: Climate sensitivity is known more precisely today than before.

98620.q: Why does the Earth not warm up to its final value immediately after a rise in CO2?
a: The oceans take up a lot of heat and react slowly
CO2 only has an effect after a hundred years
The Sun first balances out the warming
The Earth then stops radiating heat
98620.e: Water has a large heat capacity, and the deep sea warms up only slowly. That is why the warming when CO2 has doubled is smaller than the later equilibrium value.
98620.m: The sluggishness of the oceans delays the full warming.

98621.q: Why is the transient climate response smaller than the equilibrium climate sensitivity?
a: The ocean takes up a lot of heat and delays the warming
CO2 breaks down after a few years
98621.e: The deep layers of the sea warm up only slowly and store large amounts of heat. That is why the surface only reaches the full warming after centuries.
98621.m: The sluggishness of the oceans delays the full warming.

98622.q: What does comparing early climate reports from 1979 with the 2021 IPCC report on climate sensitivity show?
a: The estimate of about 3 °C was confirmed, and the uncertainty became smaller
The estimate was corrected to below 1 °C
It still cannot be estimated at all
98622.e: As early as 1979, the Charney Report estimated about 3 °C with a range of 1.5 to 4.5 °C. In 2021 the IPCC also gives 3 °C, but with the narrower range of 2.5 to 4 °C.
98622.m: As early as 1979, climate sensitivity was estimated surprisingly well.

98623.q: Which feedback amplifies the warming caused by CO2 most strongly?
a: More water vapour in warmer air
98623.e: Warm air can hold more water vapour, and water vapour is itself a greenhouse gas. Together with others, this feedback multiplies the direct CO2 warming of just over one degree.
98623.m: Feedbacks multiply the direct warming caused by CO2.

98624.q: A forcing of 4 W/m² leads to 3.2 °C of warming in the long term. What is the climate sensitivity parameter?
98624.e: The parameter is warming divided by forcing. 3.2 °C : 4 W/m² gives 0.8 °C per W/m².
98624.m: The sensitivity parameter tells you how much warming one watt per square metre brings.

98625.q: Suppose a doubling of CO2 causes 2.5 °C of warming in the long term. How much does the Earth warm if the CO2 content quadruples?
98625.e: Quadrupling corresponds to two doublings. Because forcing grows logarithmically, this gives 2 · 2.5 °C = 5 °C.
98625.m: Each further doubling of CO2 brings about the same warming.

98626.q: How far back does the EPICA ice core from Dome C in Antarctica go?
98626.e: The core covers eight cycles of cold and warm periods. Researchers at the University of Bern measured the greenhouse gases of this period in it.
98626.m: The EPICA ice tells the climate history of 800,000 years.

98627.q: At least how old is the ice that the “Beyond EPICA” project drilled in Antarctica at the beginning of 2025?
98627.e: At the Little Dome C site, the team drilled to a depth of about 2800 metres, down to the bedrock. The ice should help explain why the rhythm of the ice ages once changed.
98627.m: The oldest continuously drilled ice is over a million years old.

98628.q: What do researchers use in ice cores to determine past temperatures?
a: The ratio of heavy to light isotopes in the ice
The colour of the air bubbles
The thickness of the ice core
The salt content of the glacier water
98628.e: In a colder climate, snow contains less heavy oxygen and hydrogen. The values of oxygen-18 or deuterium therefore serve as a thermometer.
98628.m: Isotopes in ice are a thermometer of the past.

98629.q: Why is the air in the bubbles of an ice core younger than the ice around it?
a: The firn stays open for air exchange down to a greater depth
The air rises upwards in the ice
The ice melts again every summer
98629.e: Only at a depth of about 50 to 120 metres does the firn turn into dense ice and seal off the air. Until then, the air is exchanged with the atmosphere.
98629.m: There is a difference between the age of the ice and the age of the gas.

98630.q: What do ice cores from Greenland show about the climate of the last glacial period?
a: There were several rapid warmings within a few decades
The temperature stayed exactly the same the whole time
It was warmer then than today
The climate only changed every few million years
98630.e: The ice cores show abrupt climate jumps, named after the Dane Willi Dansgaard and the Bernese scientist Hans Oeschger. They are linked to changes in ocean currents.
98630.m: The climate can change very quickly, as Greenland's ice shows.

98631.q: How many years did the famous ice core from the Russian Vostok station, published in 1999, cover?
98631.e: The core showed four complete ice age cycles. CO2 and temperature rose and fell closely together in it.
98631.m: The Vostok core was the first to show several ice age cycles with CO2 values.

98632.q: According to ice cores, roughly how low was the CO2 content of the air at the height of the glacial periods?
98632.e: In the glacial periods, the oceans in particular stored more carbon. In the warm periods the value rose considerably again.
98632.m: In glacial periods the air contained much less CO2 than today.

98633.q: How can past large volcanic eruptions be recognised in ice cores?
a: By layers with a higher sulphate content
98633.e: Volcanoes release sulphur gases, which are deposited with the snow as sulphate. Such peaks also help to match up the dating of ice cores.
98633.m: Volcanic eruptions leave traces of sulphur in the ice.

98634.q: In palaeoclimatology, what are indirect climate indicators such as tree rings or pollen called?
98634.e: For the time before measuring instruments, the climate has to be worked out from natural archives. These stand-in data are calibrated against measurement series.
98634.m: Proxy data replace the missing thermometers of the past.

98635.q: Which method uses the width and density of annual rings to determine the climate and the age of wood?
98635.e: In good years trees grow more and form wider rings. By lining up many pieces of wood, calendars accurate to the year are created spanning thousands of years.
98635.m: Tree rings are climate archives accurate to the year.

98636.q: Which tiny organisms in deep-sea sediments provide data on ice volume and sea temperature with their chalky shells?
98636.e: The oxygen isotope ratio of their shells depends on water temperature and the amount of ice. Cores from the seabed therefore go back many millions of years.
98636.m: Tiny chalky shells on the seabed preserve the climate of millions of years.

98637.q: What is the rapid warm phase about 56 million years ago, in which the Earth warmed by about 5 to 8 °C, called?
98637.e: At that time, large amounts of carbon entered the atmosphere and the ocean. The event is regarded as a comparison case for today's climate change.
98637.m: The Palaeocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum shows how carbon can heat up the climate.

98638.q: What is the abrupt return to cold about 12,900 to 11,700 years ago at the end of the last glacial period called?
98638.e: After a first warming, almost ice age conditions returned to the Northern Hemisphere for about 1200 years. The phase is named after mountain avens (Dryas), a plant of cold regions.
98638.m: The Younger Dryas was a last cold snap before the Holocene.

98639.q: What is the study of pollen in lake sediments, used to reconstruct past vegetation, called?
98639.e: Pollen is preserved for a long time in deposits low in oxygen and can be assigned to individual plants. In Swiss lakes this shows, for example, the return of the forests after the ice age.
98639.m: Pollen in lake deposits reveals which plants grew in the past.

98640.q: Why are stalagmites and stalactites suitable as climate archives?
a: They grow layer by layer and store climate signals as they do so
They only grow in warm years and otherwise not at all
They contain thermometers trapped by the Romans
They change colour every day with the weather
98640.e: The chemical composition of each layer depends on temperature and rainfall. With the uranium-thorium method, the layers can also be dated precisely.
98640.m: Stalagmites and stalactites grow layer by layer and store climate signals.

98641.q: What is the hypothesis that the Earth was almost completely covered in ice about 700 million years ago called?
98641.e: Glacial deposits from this time are found even in areas that lay close to the equator then. Volcanic CO2 may later have ended the glaciation.
98641.m: The Earth was probably almost entirely covered in ice several times.

98642.q: In which city did Milutin Milanković, after whom the cycles of the Earth's orbit are named, teach as a professor?
98642.e: Milanković was a Serbian mathematician and engineer and a professor at the University of Belgrade. Over years of work by hand, he calculated solar radiation over hundreds of thousands of years.
98642.m: The Serb Milanković linked celestial mechanics and the ice ages.

98643.q: Roughly how long is the cycle in which the tilt of the Earth's axis changes?
98643.e: The obliquity of the ecliptic swings back and forth in this rhythm. A greater tilt increases the difference between summer and winter.
98643.m: The tilt of the Earth's axis varies in a rhythm of about 41,000 years.

98644.q: Between roughly which values does the tilt of the Earth's axis vary?
98644.e: Today the tilt is about 23.4° and is slowly decreasing. The Moon stabilises the axis and prevents larger variations.
98644.m: The tilt of the Earth's axis varies by only a few degrees.

98645.q: What is the approximate period of the climatically effective precession of the Earth's axis?
98645.e: Precession shifts the season in which the Earth is closest to the Sun. Together with the movement of the orbit, this gives cycles of about 19,000 to 23,000 years.
98645.m: Precession shifts the seasons along the Earth's orbit.

98646.q: What are the main periods of the change in the eccentricity of the Earth's orbit?
98646.e: Because of the pull of the other planets, the Earth's orbit becomes sometimes rounder and sometimes more elliptical. The effect on the total yearly radiation is small, but it influences the effect of precession.
98646.m: The shape of the Earth's orbit changes in cycles of hundreds of thousands of years.

98647.q: According to Milanković, which quantity is crucial for whether a glacial period begins?
a: Summer solar radiation at high northern latitudes
The strength of the Earth's magnetic field
98647.e: When summers in the north are cool, the winter snow does not melt completely and ice sheets can grow. The radiation at 65° north is often considered.
98647.m: Cool summers in the far north let ice sheets grow.

98648.q: In which month is the Earth closest to the Sun today?
98648.e: The point closest to the Sun, the perihelion, is reached at the beginning of January. Because of precession, this date moves through the year over thousands of years.
98648.m: The Earth is closest to the Sun during the northern winter.

98649.q: In what rhythm did glacial and warm periods mostly alternate over the last 800,000 years or so?
98649.e: Ice cores from Antarctica show a rhythm of about 100,000 years. Before that, there was a shorter rhythm of about 41,000 years.
98649.m: The last ice age cycles lasted about 100,000 years.

98650.q: Roughly what is the Earth's average planetary albedo?
98650.e: The Earth reflects about 30 per cent of incoming sunlight back into space. The rest is absorbed by the atmosphere and the surface.
98650.m: The Earth reflects about a third of the sunlight.

98651.q: Roughly what albedo does an open sea surface have when the Sun is high?
98651.e: Water absorbs most of the light that falls on it vertically. That is why the ocean is one of the darkest surfaces on Earth.
98651.m: The open sea is very dark and absorbs a lot of solar energy.

98652.q: On average, 340 W/m² of solar radiation reaches the Earth. How much is absorbed with an albedo of 0.3?
98652.e: The share absorbed is 1 minus 0.3, which is 0.7. 340 · 0.7 gives 238 W/m².
98652.m: The smaller the albedo, the more solar energy stays on Earth.

98653.q: Why are parts of glaciers in the Swiss Alps covered with white fleece in summer?
a: The fleece reflects sunlight and slows the melting
The fleece stores rainwater for power stations
The fleece protects animals from the cold
98653.e: The bright covering increases reflection and insulates the ice. This can greatly reduce melting on small areas, but it does not stop glaciers from shrinking.
98653.m: Bright coverings protect glaciers from melting only in small spots.

98654.q: Why does snow in the Alps melt faster when Saharan dust lies on it?
a: The dust lowers the albedo, so the surface absorbs more energy
The dust contains salt, which thaws the snow
The dust makes more rain fall
98654.e: Even a thin layer of dust makes the snow darker. It then absorbs more solar radiation and melts earlier in the year.
98654.m: Dark dust on snow speeds up melting.

98655.q: What contributes most to the Earth reflecting sunlight?
98655.e: Clouds cover about two thirds of the Earth and are bright when seen from above. They reflect more light than all surfaces together.
98655.m: Clouds are the Earth's biggest mirror.

98656.q: Why can cutting down coniferous forest in snowy northern regions have a cooling effect through the albedo?
a: Snow-covered open areas are brighter than dark conifers
Without trees there are more clouds over the sea
Snow only falls on open areas
98656.e: Dark conifers stick out of the snow and absorb a lot of light. Without them a bright snow surface remains, which counteracts the effect of the CO2 released.
98656.m: Forests affect the climate not only through CO2 but also through their brightness.

98657.q: What is the instrument called that compares incoming and reflected solar radiation to determine the albedo?
98657.e: An albedometer consists of two radiation sensors, one pointing up and one pointing down. The ratio of the two values gives the albedo.
98657.m: An albedometer measures light from above and from below.

98658.q: According to current knowledge, which feedback amplifies global warming most strongly?
98658.e: Warmer air contains more water vapour, which is itself a greenhouse gas. This amplification roughly doubles the direct warming caused by CO2.
98658.m: More warmth brings more water vapour, which warms things further.

98659.q: Why does the Earth not heat up endlessly because of extra greenhouse gases?
a: A warmer Earth radiates more heat into space
98659.e: The radiation given off by a body increases strongly with its temperature. This Planck feedback makes sure that a new, warmer balance is reached.
98659.m: More radiation when it is warm is the most important brake in the climate system.

98660.q: According to the Stefan-Boltzmann law, with which power of the absolute temperature does the heat radiation of a body grow?
98660.e: The law is j = σ · T⁴. Even if the temperature rises only a little, the radiation increases noticeably.
98660.m: Heat radiation rises with the fourth power of temperature.

98661.q: According to the IPCC, which feedback is the biggest uncertainty in estimating climate sensitivity?
98661.e: Clouds can warm or cool, depending on their height, thickness and position. The IPCC considers their overall effect likely to be amplifying, but with a wide range.
98661.m: Clouds are the biggest uncertainty in climate projections.

98662.q: How does melting ice amplify warming (ice-albedo feedback)?
a: Dark ground or water absorbs more sunlight than bright ice
Meltwater releases heat into the air
Ice produces greenhouse gases when it melts
Without ice the Earth rotates faster
98662.e: Ice and snow reflect a lot of sunlight. When the ice melts, a darker surface appears, which absorbs more energy and causes further warming.
98662.m: Less ice means less reflection and more warming.

98663.q: Warming without feedback is 1.0 °C and the feedback factor is f = 0.6. How large is the warming according to ΔT = ΔT0 / (1-f)?
98663.m: Amplifying feedbacks multiply an initial warming.

98664.q: What characterises a negative feedback in the climate system?
a: It only occurs in glacial periods
98664.e: Negative refers to the direction of the effect, not to a judgement. Such a feedback counteracts the disturbance and stabilises things.
98664.m: Negative feedbacks act like a brake.

98665.q: Why does a warmer ocean amplify warming through the carbon cycle?
a: Warm water can dissolve less CO2
98665.e: Gases dissolve better in cold water than in warm water. If the ocean warms, it takes up less CO2 and more stays in the air.
98665.m: A warm ocean absorbs less carbon dioxide.

98666.q: In which year did the IPCC's first assessment report appear?
98666.e: The first report was an important basis for the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. It was adopted in Rio de Janeiro in 1992.
98666.m: The first IPCC report paved the way for the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change.

98667.q: How did the sixth assessment report of 2021 judge human influence on the warming of the atmosphere, ocean and land?
98667.e: The report states that it is unequivocal that humans have warmed the climate system. Earlier reports had still given probabilities.
98667.m: Human influence on warming is clearly proven.

98668.q: What does IPCC Working Group II deal with?
98668.e: Working Group II studies how climate change affects people and ecosystems. It also assesses possible ways of adapting.
98668.m: Working Group II asks what climate change does and how to adapt.

98669.q: How is the Summary for Policymakers of an IPCC report adopted?
a: Line by line by government representatives by consensus
98669.e: The governments discuss the text together with the authors. The text must agree with the scientific report.
98669.m: The summary of an IPCC report is adopted jointly by all governments.

98670.q: According to the sixth IPCC report, by how much was the global surface temperature in 2011 to 2020 above the average of 1850 to 1900?
98670.e: The report gives a value of 1.09 °C. Warming was greater over land than over the ocean.
98670.m: In the decade 2011 to 2020 the Earth was about one degree warmer than before industrialisation.

98671.q: Why does the IPCC use clearly defined terms such as “likely” or “very likely”?
a: So that uncertainties are expressed consistently and comparably
So that the reports become shorter
So that non-experts do not understand the reports
Because numbers are forbidden in UN reports
98671.e: Each term stands for a fixed range, for example “very likely” for 90 to 100 per cent. So the same word means the same thing in all chapters.
98671.m: The IPCC expresses uncertainties with precisely defined terms.

98672.q: According to the sixth IPCC report, how much CO2 could still be emitted from the beginning of 2020 to keep to 1.5 °C with a 50 per cent probability?
98672.e: This remaining carbon budget corresponds to only just over a decade of today's emissions. It shrinks further every year.
98672.m: The remaining budget for 1.5 °C is very tight.

98673.q: Which special report did the IPCC publish in 2018 at the invitation of the 2015 Paris UN climate conference?
a: On the impacts of global warming of 1.5 °C
On the ice ages of the Alps
98673.e: The report compared the impacts of 1.5 °C and 2 °C of warming. It showed that even half a degree of difference has major effects.
98673.m: Every tenth of a degree of warming counts.

98674.q: What does a climate scenario such as RCP8.5 or RCP2.6 describe?
a: A possible course of greenhouse gases up to 2100
The weather forecast for next week
The number of weather stations worldwide
98674.e: RCP stands for Representative Concentration Pathway. The higher the number, the more greenhouse gases and the stronger the warming by 2100.
98674.m: The higher the number in the scenario, the stronger the warming.

98675.q: Apart from greenhouse gases, what else do the IPCC's SSP scenarios describe?
a: Possible developments in population, economy and technology
The Earth's orbit around the Sun
The height of the Alpine peaks
The position of the continents in millions of years
98675.e: SSP stands for Shared Socioeconomic Pathways. These social pathways are combined with climate forcings such as 2.6 or 8.5.
98675.m: SSP scenarios combine social development with climate forcing.

98676.q: Why is climate protection easier in a world with a lot of cooperation, education and careful use of resources?
a: Because emissions can be reduced more easily there
Because there is less sunshine there
Because greenhouse gases have no effect there
Because no energy is needed there
98676.e: In the SSP1 scenario the world focuses on sustainability. Climate protection and adaptation are then comparatively easy because countries work together and save resources.
98676.m: SSP1 is the pathway of sustainable development.

98677.q: What development is the SSP5-8.5 scenario based on?
a: Strong growth with high use of fossil energy
A rapid move away from coal, oil and gas
A sharp fall in the world's population
98677.e: SSP5 relies on technical progress and growth, driven mainly by fossil fuels. It leads to very high emissions.
98677.m: SSP5-8.5 is a scenario of very high emissions.

98678.q: According to the IPCC, roughly how much will the Earth warm by the end of the century if current trends continue?
98678.e: In the middle scenario SSP2-4.5 the best estimate is about 2.7 °C compared with 1850 to 1900. The Paris goal would clearly be missed.
98678.m: Carrying on as before leads to considerably more than 2 °C of warming.

98679.q: Which scenario of the sixth IPCC report is most likely to keep warming at around 1.5 °C by the end of the century?
98679.e: SSP1-1.9 assumes very rapid emission cuts and net zero CO2 around the middle of the century. The best estimate is 1.4 °C by the end of the century.
98679.m: Only very rapid emission cuts keep warming close to 1.5 °C.

98680.q: Why does the IPCC work with several emission scenarios instead of a single future?
a: Because future emissions depend on human decisions
Because the computers are too slow
Because every country has its own climate
98680.e: How much CO2 is emitted in future depends on politics, the economy and technology. Scenarios therefore show different possible paths.
98680.m: Scenarios show different possible climate futures.

98681.q: What are the climate scenarios for Switzerland that MeteoSwiss and ETH Zurich published in 2018 called?
98681.e: The scenarios show how temperature, rainfall and extremes in Switzerland could develop depending on the emissions pathway. Above all, they compare a future with consistent climate protection with a future without climate protection.
98681.m: Switzerland has its own regionally precise climate scenarios.

98682.q: What is the difference between an emissions scenario and a forecast?
a: It describes a possible future under certain assumptions
It predicts the future with certainty
It only relates to the past
It is based only on opinion polls
98682.e: Scenarios answer “what if” and do not give a probability of happening. Which path comes true depends on society's decisions.
98682.m: A scenario is an if-then statement about the future.

98683.q: At which university did the climate scientist Thomas Stocker head the Division of Climate and Environmental Physics from 1993?
98683.e: Stocker became a professor at the Physics Institute in Bern in 1993. The division is known for its work on ice cores.
98683.m: Thomas Stocker shaped climate physics in Bern.

98684.q: What role did Thomas Stocker have in the IPCC's fifth assessment report?
a: President of the World Meteorological Organization
98684.e: From 2008 to 2015 Stocker led the working group on the physical science basis together with a Chinese colleague. Its report appeared in 2013.
98684.m: A Swiss scientist co-led the science part of an IPCC report.

98685.q: What is the Bern climate scientist Thomas Stocker particularly known for?
a: For climate research with ice cores and his work in the IPCC
For the first ascent of Mount Everest
98685.e: Climate physics in Bern studies air bubbles in ice cores to reconstruct past climate. Stocker also led part of the fifth IPCC report.
98685.m: Thomas Stocker studies the climate using ice cores and worked in the IPCC.

98686.q: Which subject did Thomas Stocker study at ETH Zurich?
98686.e: Stocker completed his doctorate at ETH Zurich in 1987. After that he did research in London, Montreal and New York, among other places.
98686.m: Thomas Stocker is a physicist by training.

98687.q: In 2015 the Federal Council nominated Thomas Stocker to chair which international body?
98687.e: The Federal Council nominated Stocker as a candidate to chair the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. In the end, Hoesung Lee from South Korea was elected.
98687.m: In 2015 Switzerland put forward a candidate to chair the IPCC.

98688.q: Which important Swiss science prize did Thomas Stocker receive in 2017?
98688.e: The Marcel Benoist Prize is regarded as the most important science prize in Switzerland. It honoured Stocker's contributions to understanding the climate system.
98688.m: The Marcel Benoist Prize is Switzerland's highest science award.

98689.q: Which German polar explorer is the European Geosciences Union medal that Stocker received in 2026 named after?
98689.e: The Alfred Wegener Medal is one of the highest awards of the European Geosciences Union. Wegener explored Greenland and founded the theory of continental drift.
98689.m: In 2026 Stocker received the Alfred Wegener Medal.

98690.q: Which concept describes the opposite temperature trends in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres when the Atlantic circulation changes, as studied by Stocker?
98690.e: If the supply of heat to the North Atlantic weakens, the north cools while the south slowly warms. Ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica show this pattern.
98690.m: In the bipolar seesaw, north and south behave in opposite ways.

98691.q: Roughly what share of human CO2 emissions is taken up by the oceans and land ecosystems together?
98691.e: The other half builds up in the atmosphere. Without these natural sinks, the CO2 content would rise twice as fast.
98691.m: Natural sinks absorb about half of our CO2 emissions.

98692.q: What is the process called in which cold, CO2-rich surface water sinks and carries carbon into the depths?
98692.e: Cold water dissolves more CO2 and sinks at high latitudes. This brings dissolved carbon into the deep sea for a long time.
98692.m: The solubility pump carries CO2 into the depths with cold water.

98693.q: What is the transport of carbon into the deep sea by sinking remains of plankton called?
98693.e: Plankton binds CO2 through photosynthesis. Dead parts sink and hold carbon in the depths or in the sediment.
98693.m: Plankton pumps carbon into the depths of the sea.

98694.q: Which land habitat stores a particularly large amount of carbon worldwide on only about 3 per cent of the land area?
98694.e: In wet peatlands, plant remains hardly break down and build up as peat. Peatlands therefore store more carbon than all the forests on Earth put together.
98694.m: Intact peatlands are important carbon stores.

98695.q: When does a forest turn from a carbon sink into a carbon source?
a: When it gives off more CO2 than it takes up
When it is more than a hundred years old
When it has no leaves in winter
When it grows in the mountains
98695.e: Drought, fires or pests can make trees die. As the wood breaks down, more CO2 is released than the forest is still binding.
98695.m: A forest is only a sink as long as it binds more than it releases.

98696.q: What is the increased plant growth caused by a higher CO2 content in the air called?
98696.e: More CO2 makes photosynthesis easier for many plants. This explains part of the uptake by land ecosystems, but it is limited by water and nutrients.
98696.m: More CO2 makes plants grow more strongly in some cases.

98697.q: What is the technical process of filtering CO2 directly out of the surrounding air called?
98697.e: Fans suck air through filters on which CO2 is bound and later released in concentrated form. It can then be stored permanently, but the process uses a great deal of energy.
98697.m: Direct Air Capture removes CO2 from the air by technical means.

98698.q: 40 Gt of CO2 are emitted, half stays in the air, and 1 ppm corresponds to 7.8 Gt of CO2. By how much does the CO2 content rise?
98698.e: 40 : 2 = 20 Gt of CO2 stay in the air. 20 : 7.8 gives about 2.6 ppm.
98698.m: Without natural sinks the CO2 content would rise twice as fast.

98699.q: In climate policy, what is a process called that removes more greenhouse gas from the atmosphere than it releases?
98699.e: Sinks take up greenhouse gases and store them, for example in soils, biomass or seawater. Sources, on the other hand, give off greenhouse gases.
98699.m: A sink removes greenhouse gases from the atmosphere.

98700.q: Where does the water of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation mainly sink into the depths?
a: In the far North Atlantic, for example in the Labrador Sea
98700.e: There, salty surface water cools strongly and becomes heavy. It forms North Atlantic Deep Water, which flows south.
98700.m: In the far north of the Atlantic, heavy water sinks into the depths.

98701.q: Which unit measures volume flows in the ocean and equals one million cubic metres per second?
98701.e: The unit is named after the Norwegian oceanographer Harald Sverdrup. All the rivers in the world together carry only about one sverdrup of water.
98701.m: Ocean currents are measured in sverdrups.

98702.q: How much water does the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation move compared with all the rivers in the world together?
98702.e: At 26.5° north, the overturning circulation carries on average about 17 million cubic metres of water per second. All the rivers on Earth together carry only about 1 million cubic metres per second.
98702.m: The Atlantic current moves much more water than all rivers together.

98703.q: What does the sixth IPCC report expect for the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation in the 21st century?
a: A reversal of its direction of flow by 2030
98703.e: With medium confidence, the IPCC does not expect an abrupt collapse before 2100. But it does not completely rule one out.
98703.m: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation will probably weaken.

98704.q: Why does extra fresh water from Greenland weaken the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation?
a: It lowers the salt content and therefore the density of the surface water
It raises the temperature of the deep water
It slows down the Earth's rotation
98704.e: Less salty water is lighter and does not sink as easily. As a result, the driving force of the overturning becomes weaker.
98704.m: Fresh water makes seawater lighter and slows the sinking.

98705.q: What is the sea region south of Greenland that has cooled against the global trend called?
98705.e: The cold blob in the North Atlantic is often explained by a weaker supply of heat from the overturning circulation. Other causes are also being discussed.
98705.m: The cold blob in the North Atlantic could be a sign of weaker overturning.

98706.q: Why do researchers warn that the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation could tip?
a: It can have a strong and a weak stable state
The Earth's axis will soon flip
The Atlantic is slowly drying up
The Moon is slowing the current more and more
98706.e: Even Henry Stommel's simple model from 1961 showed that temperature and salt content work against each other. If a threshold is crossed, the current can switch into a weak state and stay there.
98706.m: Ocean currents can tip between two states.

98707.q: Which image is used to describe the worldwide overturning of the oceans, which distributes heat and salt?
98707.e: In the 1980s the researcher Wallace Broecker made the image of the global conveyor belt famous. It shows how water, heat and salt circulate between the oceans.
98707.m: The image of the conveyor belt made ocean circulation easy to picture.

98708.q: What effect does the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation have on the climate of north-western Europe?
a: It brings warmth and makes the winters milder
It brings cold water and cools the summers
98708.e: The current carries warm surface water north and releases heat into the air there. Westerly winds carry this heat to Europe.
98708.m: The Atlantic current is a heat pipeline to Europe.

98709.q: What do isomers always have in common?
98709.e: Isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but a different structure. That is why they usually differ in their properties too.
98709.m: Isomers have the same molecular formula but a different structure.

98710.q: How many structural isomers are there for the molecular formula C5H12?
98710.e: There are n-pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane. No further branching is possible with five C atoms.

98711.q: Besides n-butane, which compound is the second isomer with the molecular formula C4H10?
98711.e: Like n-butane, 2-methylpropane (isobutane) has four C atoms and ten H atoms, but it is branched. Cyclobutane has only eight H atoms.

98712.q: Which compound is an isomer of ethanol (C2H6O)?
98712.e: Dimethyl ether (CH3-O-CH3) also has the molecular formula C2H6O but belongs to a different class of compounds. This is called functional group isomerism.
98712.m: Ethanol and dimethyl ether have the same molecular formula.

98713.q: Why does but-2-ene have a cis and a trans isomer?
a: The C=C double bond cannot rotate freely.
98713.e: The parts of the molecule cannot rotate freely around a double bond. That is why two fixed arrangements of the methyl groups are possible.
98713.m: A double bond prevents free rotation.

98714.q: What characterises the cis isomer of an alkene?
a: Identical substituents are on the same side of the double bond.
Identical substituents are on opposite sides.
The molecule has a triple bond.
The molecule cannot be superimposed on its mirror image.
98714.e: “Cis” means on this side, “trans” means across. In the cis isomer, the identical groups are on the same side of the double bond.
98714.m: In the cis isomer, identical groups are on the same side.

98715.q: What does the letter “Z” stand for in E/Z nomenclature?
98715.e: Z comes from the German word “zusammen”, meaning together: the highest-priority substituents are on the same side of the double bond. E stands for “entgegen”, meaning opposite.
98715.m: Z means together and E means opposite.

98716.q: How many structural isomers are there for the molecular formula C6H14 (hexane)?
98716.e: They are n-hexane, 2-methylpentane, 3-methylpentane, 2,2-dimethylbutane and 2,3-dimethylbutane. With each extra C atom, the number of isomers rises sharply.

98717.q: What are isomers called that have the same connections between atoms and differ only in their spatial arrangement?
98717.e: In stereoisomers the atoms are connected in the same way but arranged differently in space. Constitutional isomers, on the other hand, differ in how the atoms are connected.
98717.m: Stereoisomers differ only in their spatial arrangement.

98718.q: When is a molecule described as chiral?
a: when it cannot be superimposed on its mirror image
when it has a double bond
when it has a plane of symmetry
98718.e: A chiral molecule cannot be made to match its mirror image by any rotation. Molecules with a plane of symmetry, on the other hand, are achiral.
98718.m: Chiral molecules cannot be superimposed on their mirror image.

98719.q: What is a typical stereocentre in organic molecules?
a: a C atom with four different substituents
a C atom with a double bond
a C atom with two identical substituents
a C atom in a benzene ring
98719.e: A carbon atom with four different bonding partners is an asymmetric C atom. It is the most common cause of chirality.
98719.m: A C atom with four different groups is a stereocentre.

98720.q: Which Greek word does the term “chirality” come from?
98720.e: The Greek word “cheir” means hand. Left and right hands are mirror images that cannot be superimposed.

98721.q: Which of these molecules is chiral?
98721.e: In butan-2-ol, the second C atom carries H, OH, CH3 and C2H5, so four different groups. In propan-2-ol two groups are the same (two CH3).

98722.q: What is a compound called that has stereocentres but is still achiral because of an internal plane of symmetry?
98722.e: One example is meso-tartaric acid. Its two stereocentres cancel each other out because of the internal symmetry.
98722.m: A meso compound is achiral despite having stereocentres.

98723.q: Which proteinogenic amino acid is not chiral?
98723.e: In glycine, the side group is just a hydrogen atom. So the central C atom carries two H atoms and is not a stereocentre.
98723.m: Glycine is the only achiral proteinogenic amino acid.

98724.q: Which letters are used under the CIP rules to give the configuration of a stereocentre?
98724.e: Under the Cahn-Ingold-Prelog rules, the substituents are ranked by priority. Depending on the direction of rotation, the centre is labelled R (rectus) or S (sinister).
98724.m: The CIP rules distinguish R and S configurations.

98725.q: What is the maximum number of stereoisomers a molecule with 3 stereocentres can have?
98725.e: The maximum is 2 to the power of n. With three stereocentres that is 2 · 2 · 2 = 8.
98725.m: With n stereocentres there are at most 2 to the power of n stereoisomers.

a: Stereoisomers that relate to each other like an object and its mirror image
Molecules that differ only by rotation
98726.e: Enantiomers are mirror images that cannot be superimposed. They only occur in chiral molecules.
98726.m: Enantiomers relate to each other like an object and its mirror image.

98727.q: In which physical property do two enantiomers differ?
a: Direction in which they rotate plane-polarised light
98727.e: Enantiomers share almost all their physical properties. However, they rotate the plane of polarised light by the same amount in opposite directions.
98727.m: Enantiomers rotate polarised light in opposite directions.

98728.q: What is a mixture of equal parts of both enantiomers called?
98728.e: A racemate contains both enantiomers in a 1 to 1 ratio. Its optical activity is zero because the rotations cancel out.
98728.m: A racemate is a 1 to 1 mixture of both enantiomers.

98729.q: Who was the first to separate enantiomers in 1848 by sorting crystals of a tartaric acid salt by hand?
98729.e: Louis Pasteur noticed that the crystals had mirror-image shapes. The separated solutions rotated polarised light in opposite directions.
98729.m: Louis Pasteur discovered the handedness of molecules.

98730.q: For which substance does one enantiomer smell of caraway and the other of mint?
98730.e: (S)-carvone smells of caraway, (R)-carvone of spearmint. The smell receptors in the nose are chiral themselves and can tell the two forms apart.

98731.q: Which instrument is used to measure how much a solution rotates polarised light?
98731.e: In a polarimeter, polarised light passes through the sample and the angle of rotation is measured. This lets you identify enantiomers and their concentration.

98732.q: Which configuration do the amino acids in the proteins of living things almost always have?
98732.e: Living things build their proteins almost entirely from L-amino acids. D-amino acids only occur in exceptional cases, for example in bacterial cell walls.
98732.m: Proteins are made of L-amino acids.

98733.q: What are stereoisomers called that are not related as object and mirror image?
98733.e: Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images, for example cis and trans isomers. Unlike enantiomers, they have different physical properties.
98733.m: Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images.

98734.q: What happens in a substitution reaction?
a: An atom or group of atoms is replaced by another.
Atoms are added to a double bond.
A small molecule is split off from a molecule.
Two molecules combine without a by-product.
98734.e: “Substituere” means to replace. So in the molecule, one atom or group is swapped for another.
98734.m: In a substitution, part of the molecule is replaced.

98735.q: Which type of reaction takes place when methane reacts with chlorine in UV light?
98735.e: The light splits chlorine molecules into radicals. In a chain reaction, an H atom of methane is then replaced by a Cl atom.
98735.m: Alkanes react with halogens by radical substitution.

98736.q: What happens in the initiation step of the radical chlorination of alkanes?
a: Light splits chlorine molecules into chlorine atoms.
Two radicals combine to form a molecule.
Hydrogen chloride breaks down into ions.
98736.e: The energy of the light splits the Cl-Cl bond homolytically. This produces two chlorine radicals, each with one unpaired electron.
98736.m: Light starts the chain reaction by splitting chlorine molecules.

98737.q: Which inorganic by-product forms when chloromethane is made from methane and chlorine?
98737.e: The equation is CH4 + Cl2 gives CH3Cl + HCl. The replaced hydrogen atom combines with the second chlorine atom.

98738.q: What happens at the attacked stereocentre in an SN2 reaction?
98738.e: The nucleophile attacks from the back while the leaving group departs. The molecule flips over like an umbrella in the wind (Walden inversion).
98738.m: In an SN2 reaction, the configuration is inverted.

98739.q: Which intermediate occurs in an SN1 reaction?
98739.e: In SN1, the leaving group departs first, forming a positively charged carbocation. Only then does the nucleophile attack.
98739.m: The SN1 reaction goes via a carbocation.

98740.q: Which haloalkane is most likely to react by the SN1 mechanism?
98740.e: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is a tertiary haloalkane. It forms a particularly stable tertiary carbocation.
98740.m: Tertiary haloalkanes prefer to react by SN1.

98741.q: Why does benzene react with bromine by substitution rather than addition?
a: The aromatic electron system is kept.
Benzene has no electrons in double bonds.
98741.e: The aromatic system is particularly low in energy and stable. It is kept in a substitution but would be lost in an addition.
98741.m: Aromatic compounds prefer substitution because the aromatic system is kept.

98742.q: Which organic product forms when bromomethane reacts with sodium hydroxide solution?
98742.e: The hydroxide ion replaces the bromine atom: CH3Br + OH- gives CH3OH + Br-. This is a nucleophilic substitution.
98742.m: Haloalkanes react with alkali to form alcohols.

a: Atoms add to a multiple bond without forming a by-product.
One atom is replaced by another.
A small molecule is split off.
An ester is split with alkali.
98743.e: In an addition, a double or triple bond is broken. All the atoms of the reactants end up in the single product.
98743.m: In an addition, two molecules form a single product.

98744.q: How does the bromine water test show a C=C double bond?
a: The bromine water loses its colour.
98744.e: The brown bromine adds to the double bond. This forms a colourless dibromoalkane.

98745.q: Which product forms when bromine adds to ethene?
98745.e: One bromine atom bonds to each of the two C atoms of the former double bond. This forms 1,2-dibromoethane.

98746.q: Which product forms when hydrogen chloride adds to ethene?
98746.e: The H atom bonds to one C atom of the double bond and the Cl atom to the other. Ethene and HCl therefore give chloroethane.
98746.m: Ethene and hydrogen chloride give chloroethane.

98747.q: According to Markovnikov's rule, which main product forms from propene and hydrogen bromide?
98747.e: The H atom goes to the C atom that already carries more H atoms. The bromine atom therefore ends up on the middle C atom.
98747.m: According to Markovnikov, the C atom with more hydrogen gets the hydrogen.

98748.q: What is the addition of hydrogen to double bonds called, which is used to harden fats?
98748.e: In hydrogenation, hydrogen is added to C=C double bonds with a catalyst such as nickel. This turns liquid oils into firmer fats.
98748.m: Hydrogenation turns unsaturated fats into saturated ones.

98749.q: Which ring-shaped intermediate occurs when bromine adds to an alkene?
98749.e: The bromine molecule is polarised by the double bond. A three-membered ring with a positively charged bromine atom forms, which is then opened by a bromide ion.
98749.m: Bromine addition goes via a bromonium ion.

98750.q: Which plastic forms when a great many ethene molecules join through their double bonds?
98750.e: In polymerisation, the double bonds open and the ethene units link up to form long chains. Polyethylene is the most widely produced plastic.
98750.m: Ethene is polymerised to make polyethylene.

98751.q: How many moles of hydrogen are needed to fully hydrogenate 1 mol of ethyne to ethane?
98751.e: Ethyne has a triple bond. Going via ethene to ethane needs two addition steps, each with 1 mol of H2.
98751.m: A triple bond can take up two molecules of hydrogen.

98752.q: What happens in an elimination reaction?
a: A small molecule is split off from a molecule and a multiple bond forms.
Two molecules join and water is split off.
One atom is replaced by another.
A molecule is added to a double bond.
98752.e: Elimination means removal. Two neighbouring atoms or groups are split off and a double bond forms between them.
98752.m: Elimination is the reverse of addition.

98753.q: Which main product forms when ethanol is heated to about 170 °C with concentrated sulphuric acid?
98753.e: The sulphuric acid removes water from the ethanol. At high temperature, elimination produces the alkene ethene.
98753.m: Removing water turns ethanol into ethene.

98754.q: According to Zaitsev's rule, which alkene is mainly formed when HBr is eliminated from 2-bromobutane?
98754.e: According to Zaitsev, the more highly substituted, more stable alkene is preferred. In but-2-ene the double bond is in the middle of the chain.
98754.m: According to Zaitsev, the more stable, more highly substituted alkene is preferred.

98755.q: What is typical of an E2 elimination?
a: The elimination happens in a single step.
98755.e: In E2, the base removes a proton while the leaving group departs at the same time. There is no intermediate.
98755.m: The E2 reaction takes place in one step without an intermediate.

98756.q: With haloalkanes and bases, which type of reaction often competes with elimination?
98756.e: A base can also act as a nucleophile. Depending on the conditions, it replaces the halogen or splits off HX.
98756.m: Substitution and elimination often compete with each other.

98757.q: Which reagent is typically used to eliminate HBr from a bromoalkane?
98757.e: A strong base in alcoholic solution removes a proton and the bromide. This reaction is called dehydrohalogenation.
98757.m: Strong bases split hydrogen halides off haloalkanes.

98758.q: Which condition favours elimination over substitution?
98758.e: Elimination turns one particle into several, so entropy increases. High temperatures make this contribution more important.

98759.q: Which product forms when hydrogen bromide (HBr) is split off from bromoethane using a strong base?
98759.e: In the elimination, an H atom and the Br atom are removed from neighbouring C atoms. A double bond forms between the two C atoms, producing ethene.
98759.m: Splitting HBr off bromoethane gives ethene.

a: a particle with a lone pair of electrons that attacks positively polarised centres
a particle that is short of electrons
a particle with no charge and no electron pair
98760.e: A nucleophile provides an electron pair for a new bond. It therefore prefers to attack atoms with a partial positive charge.
98760.m: A nucleophile donates an electron pair.

98761.q: What does the word “nucleophile” literally mean?
98761.e: “Nucleus” is Latin for kernel or core, “philos” is Greek for loving. So a nucleophile seeks positive charge like that of an atomic nucleus.

98762.e: The hydroxide ion OH- is negatively charged and has lone pairs of electrons. The other three particles are electron-poor.
98762.m: The hydroxide ion is a typical nucleophile.

98763.q: In the Lewis acid-base concept, how can a nucleophile be described?
98763.e: A Lewis base is an electron pair donor. That is exactly what a nucleophile does when it forms a bond with a carbon atom.

98764.q: Which atom of a haloalkane is attacked by a nucleophile?
a: the C atom carrying the halogen
98764.e: The halogen is more electronegative than carbon. The bonded C atom is therefore positively polarised and attracts the nucleophile.
98764.m: Nucleophiles attack the positively polarised C atom.

98765.q: Which particle is an electrophile, the counterpart of a nucleophile?
98765.e: A carbocation has a positive charge on the carbon and is short of electrons. It is attacked by particles with a lone pair of electrons.
98765.m: Electrophiles are short of electrons, nucleophiles have a lone pair.

98766.q: Why is the hydroxide ion a stronger nucleophile than the water molecule?
a: because it carries a negative charge
because it has more hydrogen atoms
because it has no lone pair of electrons
98766.e: The negative charge makes the oxygen's electron pairs more readily available. Water is neutral and therefore a weaker nucleophile.

a: the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom
the positive charge on the nitrogen
the double bond in the molecule
the electron shortage on the hydrogen
98767.e: The nitrogen atom in ammonia has a non-bonding electron pair. This allows it to form amines with haloalkanes, for example.
98767.m: Ammonia attacks with its lone pair of electrons.

a: an electron-poor particle that attacks electron-rich sites
a particle that is always negatively charged
a particle that only reacts with metals
98768.e: “Electrophile” means electron-loving. Such particles accept an electron pair, for example from a double bond.

98769.e: The nitronium ion is positively charged and electron-poor. It attacks the electron system of benzene during nitration.
98769.m: Positively charged particles such as NO2+ are electrophiles.

98770.q: Which term from the Lewis acid-base concept fits an electrophile?
98770.e: A Lewis acid is an electron pair acceptor. An electrophile accepts an electron pair when it attacks.

98771.q: Which mixture is used to produce the nitronium ion for the nitration of benzene?
a: concentrated nitric acid and sulphuric acid
hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution
98771.e: The stronger sulphuric acid protonates the nitric acid. This then breaks down into water and the nitronium ion NO2+.
98771.m: Nitrating acid supplies the electrophile NO2+.

98772.q: What does an electrophile attack in an alkene?
a: the electrons of the C=C double bond
the neutrons in the carbon nucleus
a free bonding site on the hydrogen
98772.e: The double bond is a region of high electron density. That is where the electron-poor particle attacks.
98772.m: Electrophiles are attracted by double bonds.

98773.q: Why is a carbocation a strong electrophile?
a: Its positive C atom has only six valence electrons.
It has a lone pair of electrons.
98773.e: The positively charged carbon is one electron pair short of an octet. It therefore readily accepts an electron pair.
98773.m: A carbocation is two electrons short of an octet.

98774.q: Which reaction uses aluminium chloride to introduce an alkyl group into a benzene ring?
98774.e: Aluminium chloride turns a haloalkane into a strong electrophile. This replaces an H atom on the benzene ring.
98774.m: Friedel-Crafts alkylation attaches alkyl groups to aromatic compounds.

98775.q: What role does iron(III) bromide play in the bromination of benzene?
a: It polarises the bromine molecule and makes it a stronger electrophile.
It supplies the bromine atoms for the product.
It prevents hydrogen bromide from forming.
It breaks open the benzene ring.
98775.e: Benzene is too unreactive to react with pure bromine. The Lewis acid FeBr3 draws electrons away from the bromine and creates a strongly electrophilic bromine atom.
98775.m: A catalyst can strengthen a weak electrophile.

a: Two molecules join and a small molecule such as water is split off.
Water splits a molecule into two parts.
A double bond takes up hydrogen.
98776.e: In a condensation, a new bond forms between two molecules. At the same time, water is usually released.
98776.m: In a condensation, a small molecule is split off.

98777.q: Which bond forms when two amino acids undergo condensation?
98777.e: The carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of the other, releasing water. This forms an amide bond, known as a peptide bond.
98777.m: Amino acids are linked by peptide bonds.

98778.q: Which plastic is made by polycondensation?
98778.e: Nylon is a polyamide made from a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid. A water molecule is released with each link.

98779.q: What is the reverse of a condensation called, in which a bond is split by water?
98779.e: In hydrolysis, water is taken up and a bond is split. This is how proteins are broken down during digestion, for example.
98779.m: Hydrolysis is the reverse of condensation.

98780.q: Which disaccharide forms when two glucose molecules condense via an α-1,4 bond?
98780.e: Maltose (malt sugar) consists of two glucose units. Sucrose, by contrast, contains glucose and fructose.
98780.m: Maltose consists of two glucose units.

98781.q: How many water molecules are split off when three amino acids form a tripeptide?
98781.e: Three building blocks need two peptide bonds. Each link releases one water molecule.
98781.m: With n building blocks there are n minus one peptide bonds.

98782.q: Which diol is condensed with terephthalic acid to make the plastic PET?
98782.e: PET stands for polyethylene terephthalate. It is made by polycondensation of terephthalic acid with ethanediol (ethylene glycol).
98782.m: PET is made from terephthalic acid and ethanediol.

98783.q: Which ether forms when two ethanol molecules condense with sulphuric acid at about 140 °C?
98783.e: Two ethanol molecules join through an oxygen atom and water is split off. The reaction temperature must be kept exactly.
98783.m: Two alcohol molecules can form an ether by splitting off water.

98784.q: Which substances react with each other in an esterification?
98784.e: A carboxylic acid and an alcohol form an ester. Water is the second product.
98784.m: Acid and alcohol give an ester and water.

98785.q: What is the ester made from acetic acid and ethanol called?
98785.e: The alcohol part (ethyl) comes first and the acid part (ethanoate) second. The substance is also called ethyl acetate and is a common solvent.
98785.m: Acetic acid and ethanol give ethyl ethanoate.

98786.q: Which substance is usually added as a catalyst in Fischer esterification?
98786.e: The acid protonates the carboxylic acid and makes it more reactive. Concentrated sulphuric acid also binds water.

98787.q: How can the yield of an esterification be increased?
a: by removing the water that forms
by adding the ester straight back
