99236.m: A face mask holds back droplets.

99237.q: Why should you not sneeze into your hands?
99237.e: You touch door handles and other people with your hands. That is how the germs get to others.
99237.m: Germs on your hands are quickly passed on.

99238.q: What flies out of your mouth and nose when you sneeze?
99238.e: When you sneeze, lots of tiny droplets spray out. They can contain germs.
99238.m: When you sneeze, tiny droplets fly through the air.

99239.q: What should you do when you need to cough?
a: Turn away and cough into the crook of your elbow
99239.e: You turn away from other people and cough into the crook of your elbow. That way fewer droplets reach others.
99239.m: When you cough, you turn away.

99240.q: Which illness often spreads through sneezing and coughing?
99240.e: Cold viruses are in the droplets from sneezing and coughing. That is how others catch it.

99241.q: Why do you keep your distance from people who are coughing a lot?
a: So you do not catch anything
99241.e: The droplets only fly a short distance. If you keep your distance, fewer germs reach you.
99241.m: Keeping your distance protects against infection.

99242.q: What do people in Switzerland often say when someone sneezes?
99242.e: When someone sneezes, you wish them “Gesundheit” (good health). “En Guete” is what you say before a meal.
99242.m: After a sneeze, you wish someone good health.

99243.q: Why is it better to stay at home with a fever and a cough?
a: So you do not infect others
99243.e: If you are ill, you recover faster at home. And you do not infect other children.
99243.m: If you are ill, you stay at home and protect others.

99244.q: What is a cotton bud good for, for example?
99244.e: You can use the cotton wool to paint dots of colour on paper. Cotton buds are also popular for crafts.
99244.m: You can paint dots with cotton buds.

99245.q: What is good for cleaning the outer ear when you wash?
99245.e: A damp flannel gently cleans the outer ear and behind the ear. Then you dry it well.
99245.m: You clean the outer ear with a flannel.

99246.q: Which part inside the ear can a cotton bud damage?
99246.e: The eardrum is a thin skin deep inside the ear. A cotton bud can damage it.

99247.q: Where on your ear may you use a cotton bud?
a: Only on the outside of the outer ear
99247.e: You can clean carefully on the outside of the outer ear. A cotton bud does not belong in the ear canal.
99247.m: Cotton buds are only for the outside of the ear.

99248.q: Where does a used cotton bud go?
99248.e: Cotton buds block pipes and sewage works. That is why they go in the bin.
99248.m: Cotton buds go in the bin.

99249.q: What is the tip of a cotton bud made of?
99249.e: Soft cotton wool is wrapped around the end of the stick. That is where the name comes from.
99249.m: A cotton bud has tips made of cotton wool.

99250.q: What do you do if your ear is blocked with earwax?
a: Wait a long time and say nothing
99250.e: A doctor can remove the earwax safely. Poking around in your ear yourself can hurt it.
99250.m: If your ears are blocked, the doctor can help.

99251.e: Earwax is usually yellow to brown. It is a soft, waxy substance.

99252.q: What do you wash your hair with?
99252.e: Shampoo is a liquid soap for your hair and scalp. It gets your hair clean.
99252.m: You wash your hair with shampoo.

99253.q: Do only children with unwashed hair get head lice?
a: No, it has nothing to do with dirt
99253.e: Lice climb from head to head, whether the hair is clean or not. It has nothing to do with dirt.

99254.q: Why do you close your eyes when you wash your hair?
99254.e: If shampoo gets in your eyes, it stings. With your eyes closed, that does not happen.
99254.m: Keep your eyes closed when washing your hair.

99255.q: What do you use to untangle wet hair?
99255.e: A wide-toothed comb loosens knots in your hair. You comb carefully from the bottom upwards.
99255.m: You untangle wet hair with a comb.

99256.q: What helps long hair to be combed more easily after washing?
99256.e: Conditioner makes hair soft and smooth. Then it gets fewer knots.

99257.q: Where do you massage the shampoo in well when you wash your hair?
a: On the back of your neck
99257.e: Grease and dandruff collect on the scalp. That is why you massage the shampoo in there with your fingertips.
99257.m: You massage shampoo into your scalp.

99258.q: Why should you never use a hairdryer next to a full bath?
a: You could get an electric shock
99258.e: If a hairdryer falls into the water, electricity can flow through the water. That can kill.
99258.m: Electricity and water are dangerous together.

99259.q: Why do you rinse the shampoo out well after washing?
a: So no traces stay on your scalp
99259.e: Leftover shampoo can irritate your scalp and make it itch. That is why you rinse until there is no more foam.

99260.q: How often should you change your socks?
99260.e: Your feet sweat into your socks all day. Fresh socks every day stop bad smells.
99260.m: You change your socks every day.

99261.e: Dirt, sweat and smells collect in clothes you have worn. Washing makes them clean again.

99262.q: What machine do people usually wash clothes with today?
99262.e: The washing machine washes clothes with water and washing powder. Then it spins the water out.
99262.m: Clothes are washed in the washing machine.

99263.q: What do you put on after PE?
99263.e: After sport, your PE kit is sweaty. Fresh clothes feel better and do not smell.
99263.m: After sport, you put on fresh clothes.

99264.q: What do the little pictures on a clothing label show?
99264.e: The care symbols show how warm you may wash it and whether you can iron it. That way the clothing does not get ruined.
99264.m: Care symbols tell you how to wash a piece of clothing.

99265.q: What does the number 30 in the washtub symbol on a label mean?
99265.e: The number in the washtub gives the highest washing temperature in degrees Celsius. If it is warmer, the clothing can shrink.
99265.m: The number in the washtub shows the highest washing temperature.

99266.q: Why do you not put wet clothes in the wardrobe?
99266.e: Mould grows easily in damp clothes, and they smell musty. That is why you let them dry first.
99266.m: Clothes only go into the wardrobe when dry.

99267.q: Where do you put dirty clothes?
99267.e: You collect dirty clothes in the laundry basket until they are washed. That way the clean clothes in the wardrobe stay clean.
99267.m: Dirty clothes belong in the laundry basket.

99268.q: Why do you keep your fingernails short?
99268.e: Dirt and germs get stuck under long nails. Short nails are easier to keep clean.

99269.q: What do you use to smooth rough edges on your fingernails?
99269.e: You rub the nail file gently over the edge of the nail. Then you no longer get caught on jumpers.
99269.m: A nail file smooths nail edges.

99270.q: What do you use to clean the dirt from under your fingernails?
99270.e: The small, hard nail brush gets well under the nails. With water and soap you scrub the dirt away.
99270.m: A nail brush gets your nails clean.

99271.q: Why should you not bite your fingernails?
99271.e: There are lots of germs on your fingers and under your nails. When you bite them, they go straight into your mouth.
99271.m: Nail biting puts germs in your mouth.

a: A small piece of skin sticking out at the edge of a nail
99272.e: A hangnail is a torn little piece of skin next to the nail. You cut it off carefully instead of pulling at it.
99272.m: A hangnail is a small tear in the skin by the nail.

99274.e: You collect clipped nails and throw them in the bin. That way they do not lie around.
99274.m: Clipped nails go in the bin.

99275.q: What is the right way to cut toenails?
99275.e: Toenails cut straight across do not grow into the skin so easily. Rounded corners can grow in.

99276.q: What can happen to a fingernail if you trap your finger hard?
99276.e: A bruise can form under the nail. Then the nail looks dark blue until it has grown out.
99276.m: A trapped finger can get a blue nail.

99277.q: What can you use to see bacteria?
99277.e: Bacteria are tiny and invisible to the naked eye. A microscope makes them look much bigger.
99277.m: You can only see bacteria with a microscope.

99278.q: Which food is made with the help of bacteria?
99278.e: Certain bacteria turn milk into yoghurt. The milk becomes thick and slightly sour.
99278.m: Yoghurt is made with the help of bacteria.

99279.q: Where in the body do lots of useful bacteria live?
99279.e: Countless bacteria live in the gut. They help to digest food.
99279.m: In the gut, bacteria help with digestion.

99280.q: Which medicine helps against illnesses caused by bacteria?
99280.e: Antibiotics kill bacteria or slow them down. But they do not help against viruses.

99281.e: Bacteria are living things made of just one single cell. They live almost everywhere on Earth.

99282.q: Where do bacteria especially like to multiply?
a: On hot stones in the sun
99282.e: Warmth and moisture make bacteria grow quickly. In the cold, they hardly multiply.
99282.m: Bacteria like it warm and damp.

99283.q: What can bacteria in your mouth cause if you do not brush your teeth?
99283.e: Bacteria in the mouth eat sugar and make acid. This acid attacks the teeth.
99283.m: Brushing your teeth protects against tooth decay.

99284.q: Where do used wet wipes go?
99284.e: Wet wipes do not break down in water and block the pipes. That is why you throw them in the bin.
99284.m: Wet wipes do not go down the toilet.

99285.q: What do you do after using the toilet?
99285.e: When you flush, everything goes away. Then the toilet is clean for the next person.
99285.m: Always flush after using the toilet.

99286.q: Why do you close the toilet lid before flushing?
a: So fewer splashes get into the air
99286.e: When you flush, tiny droplets splash up. A closed lid keeps them in.

99287.q: What do you often dry your hands with in a public toilet?
a: Paper towels or a hand dryer
99287.e: Public toilets have paper towels or a machine that blows warm air. That way your hands stay clean.
99287.m: In public toilets, you also dry your hands well.

99288.q: Why is it better not to take your mobile phone to the toilet?
99288.e: In the toilet, germs easily get onto your phone. Later you touch it again and hold it to your face.
99288.m: It is better to leave your phone outside when you go to the loo.

99289.q: What do you clean the toilet bowl with?
99289.e: The toilet brush stands next to the toilet. You use it to scrub dirt out of the bowl.
99289.m: The toilet brush cleans the toilet bowl.

99291.q: What do you do if the toilet roll is almost finished?
99291.e: That way the next person has enough paper too. If there is no roll, you tell an adult.
99291.m: If the paper is almost finished, you put out a new roll.

99292.q: Why do you slide down the slide by yourself?
99292.e: The Earth pulls all things towards it. This force is called gravity, and it makes you slide down the sloping slide.

99293.q: On which slide do you go faster?
a: On a very short gentle one
99293.e: The steeper the slide, the more strongly gravity pulls you along it. That is why you go faster.
99293.m: Steep slides are faster than gentle ones.

99294.q: What slows you down a little as you slide?
99294.e: When two surfaces rub against each other, it slows things down. This braking effect is called friction.

99295.q: What is the best way to brake on a slide?
99295.e: Rubber is grippy and rubs hard against the slide. That is why shoes with rubber soles brake well.
99295.m: Rubber brakes well because it is grippy.

99296.q: Why do you often slide faster on a wet slide?
99296.e: A thin film of water means you rub less against the slide. So you are slowed down less.
99296.m: Wet surfaces are often more slippery.

99297.q: Why can a metal slide be dangerous in summer?
99297.e: Metal gets very hot in strong sunshine. You can burn your skin on it, so test it with your hand first.
99297.m: Test metal in the sun with your hand first.

99298.q: Why does your hair sometimes stand on end after going down a plastic slide?
99298.e: Rubbing against plastic charges you up. Your hairs then have the same charge and push each other away.
99298.m: Rubbing against plastic can charge you up.

99299.q: Where does your speed on the slide come from?
a: From being high up at the top
From the noise of the children
From the colour of the slide
99299.e: When you climb up the ladder, you store energy by being high up. When you slide, it turns into movement.
99299.m: The higher you start, the more speed you get.

99300.q: What happens at the flat end of the slide?
a: You take off into the air
99300.e: At the flat end, gravity no longer pulls you forward. Friction slows you down until you stop.
99300.m: At the flat end the slide slows you down.

99301.q: What is an object that swings back and forth like a swing called?
99301.e: A pendulum is fixed at the top and swings back and forth. A swing is a big pendulum.

99302.q: How do you get going on a swing without being pushed?
a: Move your legs forwards and back
99302.e: If you stretch out your legs and pull them back in at the right moment, you give the swing a little energy with each swing.
99302.m: You can use your legs to get yourself going.

99303.q: Why does a swing go less and less high if nobody pushes it?
a: Air and friction slow it down
99303.e: The air and the friction at the top where it hangs slow the swing down a little. So it slowly gets smaller until it stops.
99303.m: Without a new push every swing stops.

99304.q: Where are you fastest on a swing?
a: Right at the bottom in the middle
Right at the top at the front
Right at the top at the back
99304.e: As you swing down you get faster and faster. Right at the bottom you have the greatest speed, after that you slow down again.
99304.m: A swing is fastest right at the bottom.

99305.q: Where does the swing stop for a very short moment?
99305.e: At the highest point the swing changes direction. There it stands still for a tiny moment.
99305.m: When it turns round, the swing stops briefly.

99306.q: When should you push a swing to make it go higher?
a: When it is moving away from you
When it is coming towards you
When it is hanging still and you pull
It does not matter when you push
99306.e: If you push in the same direction it is already swinging, it gets more speed. If you push against it, you slow it down.
99306.m: Always push a swing in the direction it is moving.

99307.q: Which swing swings back and forth faster?
a: The one with the biggest seat
99307.e: With a pendulum, it is mainly the length that decides how fast it swings back and forth. Short pendulums swing faster than long ones.
99307.m: Short pendulums swing faster than long ones.

99308.q: Does a heavy child on the same swing swing back and forth much more slowly than a light one?
99308.e: How fast a pendulum swings back and forth hardly depends on weight. What matters most is the length of the ropes.
99308.m: Weight hardly changes the rhythm of a swing.

99309.q: How does your body feel right at the top when the swing turns round?
99309.e: At the top, where it turns round, the seat hardly presses on you. That is why you feel very light for a moment and get butterflies in your tummy.
99309.m: At the top of a swing you feel light for a moment.

99310.q: In which direction are you pushed on a fast-spinning roundabout?
99310.e: Your body wants to keep flying straight on, but the roundabout steers you in a circle. That is why you feel a pull towards the edge.
99310.m: On a roundabout you are pulled towards the edge.

99311.q: Where on the roundabout are you moving fastest?
a: Halfway between the middle and the edge
99311.e: In one turn you travel a much bigger circle on the outside than on the inside. You have the same amount of time for it, so you are fastest on the outside.
99311.m: On the outside you spin fastest.

99312.q: Where on the spinning roundabout do you need to hold on least?
99312.e: In the middle you only turn around yourself and are hardly pulled outwards.
99312.m: The middle of the roundabout is the calmest place.

99313.q: Why do you feel dizzy after riding on a roundabout?
a: Your organ of balance is muddled
99313.e: In the inner ear there is an organ of balance with fluid in it. After spinning, the fluid keeps moving, so everything seems to spin.
99313.m: The organ of balance is in the ear.

99314.q: What does a roundabout need to start turning?
99314.e: Something that is standing still only moves when a force acts on it. On a playground roundabout, that is your push.

99315.q: What does a roundabout turn around?
a: The next piece of play equipment
99315.e: In the middle there is a fixed pole or bearing. The whole roundabout turns around it.
99315.m: A roundabout turns around its axle.

99316.q: What is the force you feel pulling you outwards on the roundabout called?
99316.e: Anyone moving in a circle feels a pull outwards. This is called centrifugal force.
99316.m: In a circle you feel centrifugal force.

99317.q: When is it safest to get off the roundabout?
a: When it is at its fastest
In the middle of a turn
99317.e: If you jump off a spinning roundabout, you take its speed with you and can fall. That is why you wait until it stops.
99317.m: Only get off when the roundabout has stopped.

99318.q: What does the mat of a trampoline do when you land on it?
99318.e: The mat gives way and is stretched downwards. Then it pulls back together and throws you up.
99318.m: A trampoline stores your energy and gives it back.

99319.q: What is attached around the edge of a trampoline between the mat and the frame?
99319.e: All the way round, many steel springs connect the mat to the frame. They stretch when you jump.
99319.m: Lots of springs hold the trampoline mat.

99320.q: Why does a garden trampoline often have a net all round it?
a: So that no rain falls in
99320.e: When jumping you can easily drift to the side. The net catches you before you fall onto the hard ground.

99321.q: How do you jump higher on a trampoline?
a: Bend your knees and push off hard
99321.e: If you bend your knees and push off hard, you press the mat down further. So it bounces you higher.
99321.m: Press the mat down further and you jump higher.

99322.q: Why is it dangerous if lots of children jump at the same time?
a: They can crash into each other
99322.e: Several jumpers disturb each other and easily bump together. That is why it is best to jump one at a time.
99322.m: On a trampoline it is best to jump alone.

99323.q: What do you call a material that goes back to its shape after being stretched?
99323.e: Elastic things such as rubber or a trampoline mat can be stretched. Afterwards they go back to their old shape.
99323.m: Elastic things spring back into shape.

99324.q: What covers the springs on a trampoline so that nobody gets hurt?
99324.e: There is a padded edge over the springs and the frame. If you land there, you do not get caught in the springs.
99324.m: The edge pad protects you from the springs.

99325.q: Where is it safest to jump on a trampoline?
99325.e: In the middle the mat bounces most evenly and you are far away from the hard frame.
99325.m: Jump in the middle of the trampoline.

99326.q: Why is it better to jump on a trampoline without shoes?
99326.e: Hard soles and little stones in the tread can wear the mat. Also, with shoes on you can hurt others more easily.
99326.m: Go on the trampoline without shoes.

99327.q: What is the place in the middle that the seesaw moves around called?
99327.e: The seesaw rests in the middle and tips around this place. It is called the pivot.
99327.m: A seesaw tips around its pivot.

99328.q: Why do many seesaws have a handle in front of the seat?
a: To hold on to when it bumps
99328.e: When the seesaw hits the bottom or reaches the top, there is a jolt. With the handle you hold on and do not fall off.
99328.m: Always hold the handle on a seesaw.

99329.q: Two children of the same weight sit equally far out. What happens?
a: One side hits the ground at once
99329.e: Both push down equally hard and equally far from the pivot. That is why the seesaw stays balanced.
99329.m: Equal weights at equal distances balance each other.

99330.q: How do you get back up on a seesaw?
99330.e: If you push off hard from the ground with your legs, your side rises. The other side then goes down.
99330.m: On a seesaw you push yourself up with your legs.

99331.q: Why is there often a piece of rubber or a car tyre under the ends of a seesaw?
a: So that the bump is soft
So that the seesaw goes faster
So that it looks more colourful
So that it does not get wet
99331.e: Without padding the seesaw would hit the ground hard. The rubber cushions the bump and protects your back.
99331.m: A rubber buffer makes the bump softer.

99332.q: What does the other side of the seesaw do when your side goes down?
99332.e: A seesaw is a straight beam with a pivot. If one end goes down, the other has to go up.
99332.m: On a seesaw one side always goes up and the other down.

99333.q: Why do you feel a jolt when your side of the seesaw hits the ground?
99333.e: You are moving down fast. When it hits the ground you are stopped very suddenly, and you feel that as a jolt.
99333.m: Stopping suddenly feels like a jolt.

99334.q: How can two small children lift an adult on a seesaw?
a: By sitting together right at the end
By sitting together in the middle
By sitting on the adult's side
By sitting apart on both sides
99334.e: Two children together are heavier than one. Right at the end of the long arm they also have the greatest leverage.
99334.m: Far out on a seesaw your weight has more effect.

99335.q: What happens if one child suddenly jumps off the seesaw while the other is up in the air?
a: The other one comes down hard
The other one flies even higher
The seesaw breaks in the middle
99335.e: Without a counterweight the seesaw tips straight down on the heavy side. The child at the top then hits the ground hard.
99335.m: Only get off once you have agreed it with each other.

99336.q: Why do you need a lot of strength in your arms when climbing?
99336.e: When you climb up, you lift your whole body. Your arms and legs work hard to do this.
99336.m: When climbing you lift your own weight.

99337.q: Why is there sand, gravel or bark chippings under a climbing frame?
a: So that a fall is softer
So that it is not dusty
99337.e: Soft ground gives way when someone falls. So you get hurt less than on tarmac.
99337.m: Soft ground protects you in a fall.

99338.q: At least how many hands and feet should be holding on when you climb?
99338.e: This is called the three-point rule: only one hand or foot moves, the other three hold on.
99338.m: When climbing, three points always hold on.

99339.q: Why are climbing frames often built from triangles?
99339.e: A triangle made of solid bars cannot be pushed out of shape without bending a bar. That makes frames especially stable.

99340.q: What should you take off before climbing in the playground?
99340.e: A bike helmet can get caught in bars or nets. Then the chin strap can become dangerous around your neck.
99340.m: Take off your bike helmet in the playground.

99341.q: Why should no cords hang down from your jacket when you climb?
99341.e: Loose cords and strings can get caught on bars or nets. That can be dangerous if you slip.
99341.m: Put loose strings away when climbing.

99342.q: What is the best way to land when you jump down from the frame?
99342.e: If you bend your knees when you land, your impact is slowed down more gently. That protects your joints and bones.
99342.m: Bend your knees when you land.

99343.q: Why does a big climbing frame not tip over when lots of children climb on it?
a: It is firmly anchored in the ground
It is tied to a tree with ropes
It is filled with air inside
99343.e: The posts go deep into the ground, often into concrete. That way the frame cannot tip over.
99343.m: Solid foundations keep play equipment safe.

99344.q: What does the seat of a zip line hang from on the cable?
99344.e: At the top of the seat there is a trolley with pulleys. The pulleys run along the tight cable.
99344.m: On a zip line a trolley rolls along the cable.

99345.q: Why do you start moving on the zip line by yourself?
a: The start is higher than the finish
The wind always blows that way
99345.e: The cable is fixed higher at the start than at the end. So gravity makes you roll down.
99345.m: A zip line slopes down from start to finish.

99346.q: Why does a zip line have pulleys instead of a simple hook?
99346.e: A hook would scrape along the cable and brake hard. Pulleys turn and glide with almost no resistance.
99346.m: Pulleys glide more easily than scraping hooks.

99347.q: What is often built in at the end of a zip line to slow you down?
99347.e: At the end the trolley bumps against a buffer with a spring or rubber. It softly absorbs the bump.
99347.m: A buffer brakes the zip line at the end.

99348.q: Why does the cable sag when a child rides on it?
99348.e: Your weight pulls down on the cable. Even a tightly stretched cable gives a little.
99348.m: Weight makes every cable sag a little.

99349.q: What should you do before you set off on the zip line?
a: Check that the way is clear
99349.e: If someone is in the way, there can be a nasty crash. That is why you only go when the way is clear.
99349.m: Only set off when the way is clear.

99350.q: What happens to you when the trolley suddenly stops at the end?
99350.e: Your body wants to keep moving, even when the trolley stops. That is why you swing forwards. This is called inertia.
99350.m: Your body wants to keep going when something brakes suddenly.

99351.q: What is the cable of a zip line usually made of?
99351.e: A steel cable is very strong and hardly stretches. It carries even heavy children safely.

99352.q: Why can you build better with wet sand than with dry sand?
99352.e: Little water bridges form between the grains. They hold the grains together, so the sandcastle stays up.
99352.m: A little water holds sand together.

99353.q: What forms when you let dry sand trickle onto a pile?
99353.e: Dry sand slides down the sides until the pile has a certain slope. That makes a cone.

99354.q: Why does water soak into sand so quickly?
a: There are gaps between the grains
99354.e: Grains of sand do not lie completely tightly together. The water runs away downwards through the many small gaps.
99354.m: Water flows through the gaps in sand.

99355.q: What happens to a sandcastle when it dries in the sun?
a: It gets as hard as stone
99355.e: The sun makes the water evaporate. Without water, the grains no longer hold together well.
99355.m: When sand dries, the castle falls apart.

99356.q: What do you use to separate fine sand from small stones?
99356.e: The sieve has small holes. The fine sand falls through, and the bigger stones stay behind.
99356.m: A sieve separates small things from big ones.

99357.q: Why do your feet sink into sand but not into tarmac?
a: The grains of sand move out of the way
99357.e: Grains of sand are loose and push aside under your weight. Tarmac is firmly joined together and does not give way.
99357.m: Loose grains give way under weight.

99358.q: Why can you pour dry sand almost like water?
a: The grains roll past each other
99358.e: The many little grains tumble over each other. That is why dry sand trickles, for example in an hourglass.
99358.m: Dry sand trickles like a liquid.

99359.q: Why does a suspension bridge wobble when you walk across it?
99359.e: A suspension bridge is not supported from below but hangs from ropes. That is why it can swing easily.
99359.m: Suspension bridges hang from ropes and swing easily.

99360.q: What happens if several children jump in time on the suspension bridge?
99360.e: Every jump in the right rhythm gives the bridge new energy, like pushing a swing. So the swinging gets bigger and bigger.
99360.m: Jumping in time makes a bridge swing harder.

99361.q: Where does a suspension bridge sag lowest?
99361.e: The ropes are fixed at the ends. In between they sag, most of all in the middle.
99361.m: The middle of a suspension bridge sags lowest.

99362.q: What is the calmest way to cross a wobbly suspension bridge?
99362.e: Calm, steady steps hardly make the bridge swing. Jumping and running make it rock.

99363.q: In which canton is the Charles Kuonen Suspension Bridge, which is almost 500 metres long?
99363.e: The Charles Kuonen Suspension Bridge near Randa in Valais is 494 metres long. It was opened for hikers in 2017.
99363.m: The Charles Kuonen Suspension Bridge is in Valais.

99364.q: What holds a suspension bridge in place at both ends?
99364.e: The ropes are anchored at both ends in solid posts or in the rock. These carry the whole load.

99365.q: Why does a suspension bridge in the playground often have nets or ropes at the sides?
a: So that you can hold on
So that birds can sit on it
99365.e: Because the bridge wobbles, you can easily lose your balance. Ropes at the sides give you something to hold and prevent falls.
99365.m: Side ropes give you a hold on suspension bridges.

99366.q: What do the ropes of a suspension bridge carry?
a: The weight of the bridge and the people
99366.e: The planks hang from the ropes. That is why the ropes carry the whole weight of the bridge and everyone crossing it.
99366.m: The ropes carry the whole suspension bridge.

99367.q: What happens if you move towards the middle of the spinning disc?
99367.e: If the weight moves closer to the middle, everything spins faster. Figure skaters use this when they pull their arms in.
99367.m: Moving weight to the middle makes a spin faster.

99368.q: Where is it easiest to push a spinning disc?
99368.e: At the edge you have a long lever to the axle. That is why you need less force there than near the middle.
99368.m: A spinning disc is easier to turn from the edge.

99369.q: Why does a well-oiled spinning disc keep turning for longer?
99369.e: Oil in the bearing lets the parts slide past each other more easily. The disc is slowed down less.

99370.q: Why should you not put your feet under the edge of a spinning disc?
99370.e: There is a narrow gap between the disc and the ground. Feet can get trapped there as it turns.
99370.m: Keep your feet away from turning parts.

99371.q: On the spinning disc, you throw a ball to a child opposite you. What do you see?
a: It seems to curve off to the side
It flies straight to the child
99371.e: While the ball is flying, the other child keeps turning with the disc. So to you it looks as if the ball is curving.
99371.m: On a spinning disc, throws seem to curve.

99372.q: You are sitting on a spinning disc. What does the playground look like to you?
a: It seems to be standing still
99372.e: Because you are spinning yourself, trees and houses move past you. It looks as if the playground is spinning.
99372.m: If you are spinning, the world seems to spin.

99373.q: One child sits at the edge, one in the middle. Who turns round more times in one full turn?
a: Both the same number of times
99373.e: Both go round exactly once when the disc turns once. The child at the edge just travels a longer way.
99373.m: On a spinning disc everyone turns the same number of times.

99374.q: Why does the disc keep turning when you stop pushing?
99374.e: Something that is moving wants to keep moving. Only friction slowly brings the disc to a stop.
99374.m: Moving things keep their momentum for a while.

99375.q: What is the best way to get up a climbing pole?
a: Pull with your arms and grip with your legs
Run up it with a run-up
99375.e: Your legs grip the pole while your arms reach higher. Then your legs push you up another bit.
99375.m: On a pole, arms and legs work together.

99376.q: Why do you slide down a smooth metal pole more easily than a rough tree trunk?
99376.e: A smooth surface hardly grips skin and clothes. So there is little friction and you slide quickly.

99377.q: Why do your hands get warm when you slide down the pole fast?
a: The sun is shining on it
99377.e: When your hands rub on the pole, heat is produced. You feel this too when you rub your hands together.

99378.q: Which workers slide down a pole in some stations?
99378.e: In some fire stations, firefighters get down a floor quickly using a sliding pole. That saves time when the alarm goes.
99378.m: Firefighters sometimes use a sliding pole.

99379.q: Why is climbing a pole harder than climbing a ladder?
a: The pole is made of rubber
99379.e: On a ladder you stand on rungs. On the pole you have to hold on just by gripping and pulling.
99379.m: Without rungs, climbing is harder work.

99380.q: Why should you never touch an icy metal pole with your tongue in winter?
99380.e: Metal draws heat out of your damp tongue very quickly. The moisture freezes at once and your tongue sticks.
99380.m: Never touch icy metal with your tongue.

99381.q: Which is easier on the pole: climbing up or sliding down?
99381.e: When you slide down, gravity helps you. When you climb up, you have to work against it.

99382.q: Why do some climbers rub white powder on their hands?
a: To make their hands smell nice
99382.e: The powder is called chalk. It soaks up sweat so that the hands do not slip.

99383.q: What is under a spring rider in the playground?
99383.e: A spring rider sits on a strong steel spring that is fixed in the ground. That is why it can rock in all directions.
99383.m: A spring rider stands on a spring.

99384.q: What does the spring do when you push the spring rider forwards?
99384.e: A bent spring always pushes back towards where it started. That is how the spring rider rocks back again.
99384.m: A spring wants to go back to its shape.

99385.q: Why does a spring rider keep rocking for a moment after you get off?
99385.e: The spring still has stored energy. It swings back and forth until the movement dies down.
99385.m: Springs keep swinging until they come to rest.

99386.q: What do you hold on to on a spring rider?
99386.e: Most spring riders have handles at the front. You hold on to them when it rocks hard.
99386.m: Always hold the handles on a spring rider.

99387.q: What does the spring under a spring rider look like?
99387.e: The spring is a thick steel wire wound up like a spiral. That way it can bend well.
99387.m: A coil spring is a wound-up wire.

99388.q: With whom does the same spring rider rock back and forth faster?
99388.e: A light child is pushed back faster by the spring. That is why the spring rider rocks in a faster rhythm with them.
99388.m: The lighter the load, the faster it bounces.

99389.q: In which directions can a spring rider rock?
99389.e: The spring is round and can bend to any side. That is why the spring rider rocks forwards, backwards and sideways.
99389.m: A spring rider rocks in all directions.

99390.q: What happens when a heavier child sits on the spring rider?
a: The spring does not bend at all
The spring bends the same amount
99390.e: More weight presses harder on the spring. That is why it gives way more than with a light child.
99390.m: More weight bends a spring more.

a: The discharge of a body of water over time
The water temperature along a river
The depth of a lake at different places
The groundwater level on a map
99391.e: A hydrograph plots discharge, usually in cubic metres per second, against time. This shows how a body of water reacts to rain or snowmelt.
99391.m: A hydrograph shows how discharge changes over time.

99392.q: In which unit is the discharge of a river usually given in a hydrograph?
99392.e: Discharge is a volume flow, that is, volume per time. For rivers, cubic metres per second are usually used, and for small streams also litres per second.
99392.m: Discharge is measured as volume per time.

99393.q: What is the highest point of a flood hydrograph called?
99393.e: At the peak, discharge reaches its maximum during an event. After that, the falling limb of the hydrograph begins.
99393.m: The peak is the highest discharge during a flood.

99394.q: In a hydrograph, what is meant by base flow?
a: The share that keeps flowing in from groundwater even without rain
The discharge directly after a thunderstorm
The water that evaporates at the surface
The maximum discharge in a once-in-a-century flood
99394.e: Base flow comes mainly from groundwater and other slow stores. It keeps a river flowing even in dry periods.
99394.m: Base flow is fed by groundwater.

99395.q: What is the time between the peak of rainfall and the peak of discharge called?
99395.e: The water needs time to reach the measuring point over the ground and through channels. This delay, the lag time, is short in small, steep catchments.
99395.m: The shorter the lag time, the faster a river reacts to rain.

99396.q: How does a large amount of sealed ground in the catchment change the flood hydrograph?
a: The peak becomes higher and comes earlier
The peak becomes lower and comes later
99396.e: On sealed surfaces, rain cannot soak in and runs off quickly over the surface. As a result, discharge rises faster and reaches higher peaks.
99396.m: Sealed surfaces make floods faster and higher.

99397.q: What does the falling limb (recession limb) of a hydrograph describe?
a: The gradual emptying of the stores after the event
The rise in discharge during the rain
The growth of the snow cover
99397.e: After the peak, discharge decreases because soil and groundwater stores slowly release water. The shape of this limb reveals a lot about the stores of a catchment.
99397.m: The recession limb shows how the stores drain after an event.

99398.q: When does a heavily glaciated Alpine river in Switzerland typically reach its average peak discharge over the year?
99398.e: In a glacial discharge regime, the melting of ice and snow supplies the most water in the warm summer months. In winter the discharge is very low.
99398.m: Glacier rivers carry the most water in high summer.

99399.q: In a flood event, which amount of water does the area between the hydrograph and the base flow correspond to?
a: The total evaporation in the year
99399.e: The area under a curve of discharge times time gives a volume. Above the base flow, this is the part of the rain that runs off quickly.
99399.m: The area under the hydrograph is a volume of water.

99400.q: Which quantity completes the water balance equation “precipitation equals runoff plus evaporation plus ...”?
99400.e: What falls as precipitation runs off, evaporates or is stored for a time, for example in groundwater, lakes, snow or glaciers. Over long periods, the change in storage is often close to zero.
99400.m: The water balance also takes the change in storage into account.

99401.q: What is meant by evapotranspiration in the water balance?
a: The sum of evaporation from surfaces and transpiration by plants
99401.e: Evaporation is water evaporating from soil and water surfaces; transpiration is plants giving off water through their stomata. Together they make up evapotranspiration.
99401.m: Evapotranspiration combines evaporation and plant transpiration.

99402.q: In a catchment, 1200 mm of precipitation falls in a year, 500 mm evaporates and the stores stay the same. How large is the runoff depth?
99402.e: Runoff equals precipitation minus evaporation minus change in storage: 1200 mm minus 500 mm minus 0 mm gives 700 mm.
99402.m: Without a change in storage, runoff is the difference between precipitation and evaporation.

99403.q: A river carries 10 cubic metres per second on average over the year, and its catchment measures 315.36 square kilometres. How large is the annual runoff depth?
99403.e: Annual volume: 10 cubic metres times 31,536,000 seconds gives 315,360,000 cubic metres. Divided by an area of 315,360,000 square metres this gives 1 m, that is, 1000 mm.
99403.m: Runoff depth is the volume of runoff divided by the area of the catchment.

99404.q: What does the runoff coefficient indicate?
a: The share of precipitation that runs off
The speed of the water in the river
The width of a river bed
The amount of salt in the river water
99404.e: The runoff coefficient is the ratio of runoff to precipitation. On tarmac it is close to 1, on forest soil much lower.
99404.m: A high runoff coefficient means that little water soaks in or evaporates.

99405.q: Roughly what is the long-term average annual precipitation in Switzerland?
99405.e: According to the Hydrological Atlas of Switzerland, just over 1400 mm falls per year on average across the country. More than half of it runs off, and most of the rest evaporates.
99405.m: With about 1400 mm of precipitation a year, Switzerland is a wet country.

99406.q: Why is Switzerland often called the “water tower of Europe”?
a: Because large rivers such as the Rhine and the Rhône rise there and a lot of water is stored there
Because it desalinates most of Europe's seawater
Because it does not pass on any rivers to neighbouring countries
Because there are never any dry periods there
99406.e: The Rhine, the Rhône and the Inn rise in Switzerland, as do tributaries of the Po. Lakes, glaciers and groundwater store a significant part of Europe's fresh water.
99406.m: Through its rivers, Switzerland passes on a lot of water to the whole of Europe.

99407.q: What is true of the water balance of the oceans in the long term?
a: More water evaporates over them than falls there as precipitation
More precipitation falls over them than evaporates
They lose a lot of volume every year
They take in no river water
99407.e: The surplus of evaporation over the oceans is carried to the continents as water vapour. There it falls as precipitation and flows back into the sea through the rivers.
99407.m: Rivers return to the oceans the water that evaporates there more than it rains.

99408.q: What does the climatic water balance describe?
99408.e: If the climatic water balance is negative, more water can evaporate at that place than falls as rain. It is used, for example, to assess drought stress in farming.
99408.m: A negative climatic water balance points to dryness.

a: A body of rock with cavities that can carry groundwater
A pipe that pumps groundwater to houses
99409.e: Aquifers have pores, fissures or karst cavities through which water can flow. Layers with low permeability, such as clay, are called aquitards or aquicludes instead.
99409.m: An aquifer stores and carries groundwater.

99410.q: Which type of aquifer is typical of the gravel and sand deposits of the large Swiss river valleys?
99410.e: In loose rocks such as gravel, water flows through the pores between the grains. Such valley gravels are among the most productive groundwater sources in Switzerland.
99410.m: In gravel and sand, groundwater flows through the pores.

99411.q: Which loose sediment typically has the greatest permeability for groundwater?
99411.e: Gravel has large, well-connected pores, and its hydraulic conductivity is very high. Clay has a lot of pore space, but tiny pores through which water hardly flows.
99411.m: The larger the grains, the more permeable a loose sediment usually is.

99412.q: Which law describes the flow of groundwater through porous rock?
99412.e: According to Henry Darcy, the flow is proportional to the permeability, the cross-sectional area and the hydraulic gradient. The law dates from 1856.
99412.m: Darcy's law links permeability, area and gradient with the flow.

99413.q: According to Darcy's law, the flow Q equals permeability times cross-section times gradient. What is Q with 0.001 m/s, 100 square metres and a gradient of 0.01?
99413.e: 0.001 times 100 times 0.01 gives 0.001 cubic metres per second. This corresponds to 1 litre per second.
99413.m: The Darcy flow is the product of permeability, area and gradient.

99414.q: According to the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN), what share of drinking water in Switzerland comes from groundwater (including spring water)?
99414.e: The Federal Office for the Environment states that about four fifths of drinking water is obtained from groundwater. Most of the rest comes from lake water.
99414.m: Most Swiss drinking water is groundwater.

a: An aquifer beneath an impermeable cover layer whose water is under pressure
An aquifer whose surface is freely connected to the air
99415.e: With confined groundwater, the water level in a borehole rises above the top of the aquifer. If it is even above the ground, an artesian well flows by itself.
99415.m: Confined groundwater is under pressure and rises in boreholes.

99416.q: What forms around a well from which groundwater is pumped?
99416.e: Pumping makes the groundwater level around the well sink in the shape of a funnel. As a result, water flows towards the well from all sides.
99416.m: Pumping creates a cone of depression in the groundwater level.

99417.q: Which chemical process creates karst cavities in limestone?
a: Limestone being dissolved by water containing carbonic acid
Limestone melting because of the Earth's heat
Limestone being oxidised by oxygen in the air
99417.e: Water takes up CO2 from the air and soil and forms carbonic acid. This dissolves calcium carbonate into dissolved calcium hydrogen carbonate.
99417.m: Water containing carbonic acid dissolves limestone and creates karst caves.

99418.q: How does a typical karst spring react to heavy rain?
a: The amount of water rises quickly and sharply
The amount of water stays exactly the same
It only reacts after several years
99418.e: In karst areas, water flows quickly to the spring through large tubes and fissures. That is why the amount of water varies greatly and often reacts within hours.
99418.m: Karst springs vary greatly and react quickly to rain.

99419.q: What is the amount of water a spring delivers per unit of time called?
99419.e: The yield of a spring is given, for example, in litres per second. In karst springs it can vary many times over between dry and wet periods.
99419.m: The yield is how productive a spring is.

99420.q: What does the water of many karst springs often look like shortly after heavy rain?
99420.e: The fast inflow through open karst tubes washes soil particles and sediments along with it. That is why karst springs often become cloudy after heavy rainfall, which makes them harder to use for drinking water.
99420.m: After heavy rain, karst springs are often cloudy.

99421.q: Which method is used to find out where the water of a karst spring comes from?
99421.e: A harmless dye such as uranine is put into the water at a place where it soaks away. If it appears at a spring, the underground connection is proven.
99421.m: Tracer tests reveal underground flow paths in karst.

99422.q: Which spring near Vallorbe is fed underground with water from the area of Lac de Joux and Lac Brenet?
99422.e: The water from the Vallée de Joux soaks away into sinkholes in the limestone. It comes back to the surface near Vallorbe as the karst spring of the Orbe.
99422.m: The Orbe disappears underground in the Vallée de Joux and reappears near Vallorbe.

99423.q: What is a place where a stream in karst disappears underground called?
99423.e: At swallow holes or ponors, a surface stream drains into karst cavities. The water often reappears at a karst spring kilometres away.
99423.m: In a swallow hole, a stream disappears into karst rock.

99424.q: Where does most of the Danube water that soaks away near Immendingen reappear?
a: In the Aachtopf in the Hegau
In the source of the Rhône
In the source of the Neckar
99424.e: A large part of the Danube water soaks away into the limestone of the Swabian Jura. It appears in the Aachtopf, Germany's largest spring, and flows via the Radolfzeller Aach to the Rhine.
99424.m: Some Danube water reaches the Rhine through the karst.

99425.q: At what temperature does fresh water have its greatest density?
99425.e: This density anomaly of water is crucial for the layering and mixing of lakes and explains why lakes freeze from the top down.
99425.m: Fresh water is densest at about 4 °C.

99426.q: In which seasons does a typical lake in the Swiss Plateau mix completely?
99426.e: In spring and autumn the water is about the same temperature from top to bottom. The wind can then overturn the whole lake, while in summer and winter it is layered.
99426.m: Many lakes mix in spring and autumn.

99427.q: Why is there often no oxygen in the deep water of a lake that never mixes with the surface water?
a: It is used up as dead material breaks down and is not replaced
Because fish carry it down into the depths
Because water cannot dissolve oxygen at depth
Because the oxygen sinks to the lake bed and soaks away
99427.e: Bacteria break down dead algae and animals on the bottom and use up oxygen in the process. Without mixing, no fresh oxygen reaches the bottom from the surface.
99427.m: Without mixing, the deep water of a lake stays low in oxygen.

99428.q: Which Swiss lake is known for its northern basin not having mixed completely for decades?
99428.e: The deep northern basin of Lake Lugano was meromictic for a long time, and its deep water remained without oxygen. Only in cold winters such as 2005 and 2006 did it mix as an exception.
99428.m: The northern basin of Lake Lugano only rarely circulates completely.

99429.q: What triggers autumn overturn in a lake?
a: The surface water cools, becomes denser and sinks
The deep water is warmed by the Earth's heat
99429.e: In autumn the top layer cools until it is as dense as the deep water. Then the wind is enough to mix the whole lake.
99429.m: Cooling in autumn breaks up a lake's summer layering.

99430.q: Why is complete mixing of a lake important for life in the lake?
a: It brings oxygen to the depths and nutrients to the top
It increases the salt content of the lake
It prevents algae from forming for ever
99430.e: During layering, oxygen is used up in the deep water and nutrients build up. Circulation evens this out and supplies the whole lake again.
99430.m: Lake circulation supplies the deep water with oxygen.

99431.q: How is a frozen lake layered by temperature in winter?
a: Cold water around 0 °C at the top, water at about 4 °C at the bottom
4 °C at the top, 0 °C at the bottom
10 °C at the top, 0 °C at the bottom
99431.e: Under the ice, the coldest, lighter water lies at the top. The densest water, at about 4 °C, collects at the bottom; this is called inverse layering.
99431.m: Under the ice, the water at the bottom of the lake is warmer than at the surface.

99432.q: How is a deep lake layered in summer?
a: Warm water at the top, cold water at the bottom
Cold water at the top, warm water at the bottom
99432.e: The Sun warms the surface water, which is lighter and stays at the top. In the depths, the cold, denser water at about 4 °C stays put.
99432.m: In summer, warm water lies above cold deep water.

a: A layer of water in which the temperature falls sharply with depth
A line of equal air temperature on a weather map
A warm ocean current at the surface
A layer with constant salt content
99433.e: The thermocline separates warm surface water from cold deep water. In it, the temperature changes greatly over a short distance.
99433.m: The thermocline is a layer where the temperature changes sharply.

99434.q: What is the cool layer of water below the thermocline of a layered lake called?
99434.e: In summer a layered lake is divided into three storeys; the lowest layer lies below the thermocline. It is cold and hardly mixed by the wind.
99434.m: The hypolimnion is the cold deep layer of a lake.

99435.q: What is the warm surface layer of a lake in summer, mixed by the wind, called?
99435.e: The epilimnion is warmed by the Sun and stirred by the wind. Below it comes the metalimnion with the thermocline.
99435.m: The epilimnion is the warm top layer of a lake.

99436.q: Roughly at what depth range does the permanent thermocline lie in tropical and temperate oceans?
99436.e: Below the mixed surface layer, the temperature in the ocean falls sharply down to a depth of about 1000 m. Below that, the deep water is cold and changes only a little.
99436.m: The permanent thermocline in the ocean lies below the surface layer down to about 1000 m.

99437.q: Why is there usually no clear thermocline in polar seas?
a: Because the surface water is almost as cold as the deep water
Because the sea there is over 20 °C everywhere
Because polar seas have no wind
Because there is no salt in the water there
99437.e: At high latitudes the Sun hardly warms the surface water. Without a warm lid there is no strong temperature difference, and the layering there is determined more by salt content.
99437.m: In polar seas there is little temperature difference between top and bottom.

99438.q: What does the density of seawater mainly depend on?
a: On wave height and wind direction
99438.e: Cold, salty water is denser than warm water with little salt. These differences in density drive the great deep currents of the oceans.
99438.m: Cold and salt make seawater denser.

99439.q: What effect does a strong thermocline have on the exchange of substances in the water?
a: It slows down the exchange of nutrients and oxygen between top and bottom
It speeds up mixing down to the bottom
It turns fresh water into salt
99439.e: The stable layering by density acts like a barrier. Nutrients from the depths hardly reach the top, and oxygen hardly reaches the bottom.
99439.m: A thermocline separates surface and deep water like a barrier layer.

99440.q: Why does it suddenly get much colder below a certain depth when diving in a lake in summer?
a: You dive through the thermocline into the cold deep water
Because a cold spring rises there
Because the water is saltier at depth
Because the wetsuit no longer keeps you warm at depth
99440.e: In summer, warm surface water lies above cold deep water. In between, in the thermocline, the temperature drops sharply over a short distance.
99440.m: In the thermocline the water quickly gets colder.

99441.q: What is meant by eutrophication of a body of water?
a: Enrichment with nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen
99441.e: Nutrients get into the water through fertiliser and sewage. This encourages excessive growth of algae and water plants.
99441.m: Eutrophication means over-fertilisation of a body of water.

99442.q: Which nutrient limits algae growth in most Swiss lakes?
99442.e: In freshwater lakes, phosphorus is usually the scarce nutrient. Even small extra amounts of phosphorus therefore trigger strong algae growth.
99442.m: In lakes, phosphorus is usually the limiting nutrient.

99443.q: Which measure came into force in Switzerland in 1986 to reduce the over-fertilisation of lakes?
a: The ban on phosphates in laundry detergents
A ban on motorboats on all lakes
A ban on swimming in all lakes
99443.e: Phosphates from detergents were a main source of over-fertilisation in lakes. Together with the expansion of sewage treatment plants, the phosphorus levels of many lakes then fell considerably.
99443.m: Since 1986, laundry detergents in Switzerland must not contain phosphate.

99444.q: Why is there often no oxygen in the deep water of eutrophic lakes?
a: Bacteria use up a lot of oxygen when breaking down dead algae
Algae give off carbon monoxide in the deep water
The pressure squeezes the oxygen out of the water
99444.e: Dead algae sink into the depths and are broken down there. This breakdown uses up the oxygen, especially when the lake is layered in summer.
99444.m: The breakdown of lots of algae uses up the oxygen in the deep water.

99445.q: What is a clear lake with few nutrients called?
99445.e: The trophic levels range from oligotrophic through mesotrophic and eutrophic to hypertrophic. Many Alpine lakes are naturally oligotrophic.
99445.m: Oligotrophic lakes are low in nutrients and clear.

99446.q: How do Swiss sewage treatment plants remove phosphate from waste water in the chemical treatment stage?
a: By precipitation with iron or aluminium salts
99446.e: Iron or aluminium salts form compounds with phosphate that hardly dissolve. These settle as sludge and are removed from the water in this way.
99446.m: Phosphate is precipitated chemically in sewage treatment plants.

99447.q: With which measure have lakes in Lucerne such as Lake Baldegg and Lake Sempach been supported since the 1980s?
a: With artificial aeration and oxygen supply
By covering them with floating sheets
99447.e: Because of over-fertilisation, the deep water of these lakes lacked oxygen. Aeration and adding oxygen are used to improve the deep water until the nutrient load falls.
99447.m: Aeration helps over-fertilised lakes but does not replace reducing nutrients.

99448.q: Which cyanobacterium can turn lakes such as Lake Murten reddish and is named after a battle?
99448.e: Planktothrix rubescens turns the water reddish when it multiplies in large numbers. The name recalls the legend that Lake Murten was red with the blood of the Burgundians after the Battle of Murten in 1476.
99448.m: The Burgundy blood alga can turn lakes red.

99449.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, wind drives the top layer of the sea. Because of the Coriolis force, the water is deflected overall (Ekman transport). In which direction?
a: At right angles to the right of the wind
At right angles to the left of the wind
Exactly in the direction of the wind
99449.e: Overall, the wind-driven surface layer is carried not in the direction of the wind but at right angles to it. In the Northern Hemisphere the Coriolis force deflects to the right.
99449.m: In the Northern Hemisphere, Ekman transport carries water to the right of the wind.

99450.q: In the Southern Hemisphere, wind blows over the sea. In which direction does the Coriolis force deflect the driven surface water overall?
a: To the left of the wind direction
To the right of the wind direction
Not at all, it flows with the wind
99450.e: In the Southern Hemisphere the Coriolis force acts to the left. That is why the water moved by the wind is deflected to the left overall there.
99450.m: In the Southern Hemisphere the Coriolis force deflects the water to the left.

99451.q: Which two influences together produce Ekman transport?
a: Wind friction and the Coriolis force
Tidal force and the Earth's heat
99451.e: The wind drives the surface, and friction passes the momentum downwards. The Coriolis force deflects each layer further, so that a balance is reached.
99451.m: Ekman transport results from wind friction and the Coriolis force.

99452.q: What does the Ekman spiral describe?
a: The turning of the current's direction with increasing depth
The shape of a deep-sea trench
99452.e: Each deeper layer is driven by the one above it and deflected further. The arrows of the current therefore turn in a spiral with depth.
99452.m: In the Ekman spiral the current turns with depth.

99453.q: How does the speed of the current in the Ekman spiral change with increasing depth?
a: It is greatest at the bottom
99453.e: Because of friction, each deeper layer loses momentum. Below the Ekman layer the wind-driven current has almost disappeared.
99453.m: The Ekman current gets weaker with depth.

99454.q: Why is the surface water of the sea not carried exactly in the direction of the wind?
a: The Earth's rotation deflects the moving water sideways
The water is attracted by the Moon
The salt slows the water down on one side
99454.e: The Coriolis force is caused by the Earth's rotation and deflects moving water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
99454.m: The Coriolis force deflects ocean currents away from the wind.

99455.q: Which polar explorer observed that drift ice did not drift exactly with the wind, which led to the Ekman theory?
99455.e: On the Fram expedition, Nansen noticed that the ice drifted to the right of the wind direction. Vagn Walfrid Ekman explained this mathematically in 1905.
99455.m: Nansen's observation of drift ice led to the Ekman theory.

99456.q: Why does floating plastic waste collect in the large subtropical ocean gyres?
a: Ekman transport carries the surface water towards the centre of the gyres
The water at the centre is free of salt
There is no Coriolis force there
99456.e: In the subtropical gyres, the winds drive the water towards the middle through Ekman transport. Floating objects build up there, for example in the Great Pacific Garbage Patch.
99456.m: Ekman convergence collects floating debris in the middle of ocean gyres.

99457.q: What happens in the equatorial Pacific during an El Niño event?
a: The surface water in the central and eastern Pacific becomes unusually warm
The water off Peru becomes unusually cold
99457.e: During El Niño, warm water spreads east from the western Pacific. This changes air pressure, winds and rainfall worldwide.
99457.m: El Niño brings warm water to the eastern Pacific.

99458.q: Where does the name El Niño come from?
a: From Peruvian fishermen, because the warm water often appeared around Christmas
From a ship that discovered the effect
From an island in the Atlantic
99458.e: In Spanish, El Niño means “the boy” and refers to the Christ Child. The warming off the coast of Peru often appeared around Christmas time.
99458.m: El Niño is named after the Christ Child.

99459.q: What is the cool counterpart of El Niño called?
99459.e: During La Niña the trade winds are stronger and the water in the eastern Pacific is colder than normal. Together with El Niño, it forms the two extremes of the same climate phenomenon.
99459.m: La Niña is the cold phase of the ENSO phenomenon.

99460.q: What does the abbreviation ENSO stand for?
99460.e: ENSO links the ocean warming El Niño with the Southern Oscillation, a seesaw in air pressure between Tahiti and Darwin. Ocean and atmosphere are closely coupled.
99460.m: ENSO links ocean and atmosphere in the tropical Pacific.

99461.q: What happens to the trade winds over the equatorial Pacific during El Niño?
99461.e: Normally the trade winds push warm water westwards. When they weaken, the warm water sloshes back to the east.
99461.m: During El Niño the trade winds weaken.

99462.q: What effect does El Niño typically have on fishing off Peru?
99462.e: Warm surface water suppresses the upwelling of nutrient-rich deep water. As a result there is a lack of plankton, and the fish stocks off Peru decline sharply.
99462.m: El Niño weakens fishing off Peru.

99463.q: Roughly how often do El Niño events occur?
99463.e: El Niño is not strictly periodic; it occurs irregularly about every two to seven years. An event usually lasts nine to twelve months.
99463.m: El Niño returns irregularly every few years.

99464.q: How does the thermocline in the eastern equatorial Pacific change during El Niño?
99464.e: Because warm water collects in the east, the thermocline sinks there. Water that wells up then comes from the warm, nutrient-poor layer above.
99464.m: During El Niño the thermocline off South America is pushed down.

99465.q: Roughly what is the average salinity of seawater?
99465.e: One kilogram of seawater contains on average about 35 grams of dissolved salts. This is also written as 35 per mille or as a practical salinity of 35.
99465.m: Seawater contains on average about 3.5 per cent salt.

99466.q: Which ion makes up the largest share by mass of the dissolved salts in seawater?
99466.e: Chloride makes up about 55 per cent of the mass of dissolved salt, sodium about 30 per cent. Together they correspond to table salt.
99466.m: Chloride is the most common ion in seawater.

99467.q: Which marginal sea is especially salty, with values around 40 grams per kilogram, because of strong evaporation and little inflow?
99467.e: A lot of water evaporates in the Red Sea, and hardly any rivers flow into it. That is why it is one of the saltiest seas with open access to the ocean.
99467.m: The Red Sea is especially salty.

99468.q: Why is the Baltic Sea a brackish sea with low salinity?
a: Many rivers bring fresh water, and exchange with the North Sea is small
Because sea ice melts there every day
Because it is deeper than the Atlantic
99468.e: The Baltic Sea receives a lot of fresh water from rivers and precipitation. Salty North Sea water only gets in through the narrow Danish straits.
99468.m: Plenty of fresh water and little exchange make the Baltic brackish.

99469.q: How is salinity in the sea usually measured today?
a: Through the electrical conductivity of the water
Through the cloudiness of the water
Through the colour of the water
Through the pH of the water
99469.e: Dissolved ions conduct electricity: the more salt, the higher the conductivity. The 1978 Practical Salinity Scale is based on this relationship, corrected for temperature and pressure.

99470.q: Why is seawater denser than fresh water?
a: Because salts are dissolved in it
Because it is always colder than fresh water
Because it contains more air bubbles
Because it is coloured green by algae
99470.e: The dissolved salts increase the mass per volume. That is why it is easier to float in the sea than in a lake.

99471.q: What does the principle of constant proportions state for seawater?
a: The ratios of the main ions are almost the same everywhere
Every ocean has exactly the same salinity
The salt content always increases with depth
Salt and water evaporate at the same rate
99471.e: Even if the total salt content varies, the ratios of, for example, chloride, sodium and sulphate stay constant. That is why the total salinity can be worked out from one component.
99471.m: The main ions in seawater are in fixed ratios to each other.

99472.q: What happens to the salinity of the surrounding water when sea ice forms?
a: It rises, because most of the salt is pushed out during freezing
The water turns into fresh water
99472.e: Ice crystals take in hardly any salt, and the brine goes into the water below. This becomes heavier and sinks, which helps to form deep water.
99472.m: When sea ice forms, the water below becomes saltier and heavier.

99473.q: Why is surface salinity especially high in the subtropics?
a: More water evaporates there than falls as precipitation
The largest rivers flow into the sea there
99473.e: In the subtropical high-pressure areas it is dry and sunny. The strong evaporation concentrates the salt at the surface.
99473.m: High evaporation raises the salt content at the sea surface.

99474.q: What happens in an upwelling area in the ocean?
a: Cold, nutrient-rich deep water rises to the surface
Warm surface water sinks into the deep sea
Fresh water flows up from the seabed
99474.e: In upwelling, water from the depths replaces surface water that has been carried away. It brings nutrients such as nitrate and phosphate into the light.
99474.m: In upwelling areas, nutrient-rich deep water comes to the top.

99475.q: On which coasts are the large coastal upwelling areas typically found?
a: On the west coasts of the continents at low latitudes
On the east coasts in the polar regions
Only on islands in the Indian Ocean
99475.e: Examples are the coasts off Peru and Chile, Namibia, California and north-west Africa. There, winds blow parallel to the coast towards the equator.
99475.m: Large upwelling areas lie on the west coasts of the continents.

99476.q: Why do winds along the coast cause upwelling off Peru?
a: Ekman transport carries surface water away from the coast
The wind pushes water towards the coast
The tides pump water up from the depths
99476.e: Winds blowing parallel to the coast towards the equator carry the surface water out to the open sea through Ekman transport. Cold deep water flows in from below to replace it.
99476.m: Offshore Ekman transport creates coastal upwelling.

99477.q: Why are upwelling areas so important for fishing?
a: The nutrients make a great deal of plankton grow
The water there is especially warm
There are no predatory fish there
The water there is free of salt
99477.e: Plankton forms the basis of a rich food chain. Although upwelling areas make up only a small part of the sea's surface, a large part of the world's fish catch comes from there.
99477.m: Upwelling areas are among the most productive regions of the sea.

99478.q: Which fish species is caught in especially large quantities in the upwelling area of the Humboldt Current?
99478.e: The Peruvian anchovy (anchoveta) forms huge shoals in the cold, nutrient-rich water off Peru. It is mainly processed into fishmeal and fish oil.
99478.m: The anchoveta lives on the plankton of the Humboldt upwelling.

99479.q: Why is there upwelling at the equator in the Pacific?
a: Ekman transport carries water away to the north and south of the equator
The Coriolis force is strongest at the equator
The sea is shallowest at the equator
Most rivers flow into the sea there
99479.e: The trade winds blow westwards on both sides of the equator. Ekman transport deflects the surface water towards the poles on both sides, and this divergence sucks deep water up.
99479.m: At the equator the Ekman transports move apart and cause upwelling.

99480.q: Why are there often deserts such as the Atacama or the Namib on coasts with strong upwelling?
a: Cold upwelling water cools the lower air and stabilises it, so hardly any rain falls
The sea releases salt into the air there, which prevents rain
99480.e: Over cold water, a stable layering of air with an inversion forms. Moist air can hardly rise, so no rain clouds form.
99480.m: Cold upwelling water encourages coastal deserts.

99481.q: Which weather phenomenon is especially common on coasts with cold upwelling water?
99481.e: When moist sea air cools over cold water, it condenses into fog. In Chile this fog is called camanchaca and is partly harvested with fog nets.
99481.m: Coastal fog often forms over cold upwelling water.

99482.q: At which plate boundaries do deep-sea trenches form?
a: At hotspots in the middle of a plate
At transform faults with no movement
99482.e: A deep-sea trench forms where one oceanic plate sinks beneath another. Volcanic arcs and strong earthquakes nearby are typical.
99482.m: Deep-sea trenches mark zones where a plate sinks.

99483.q: Which deep-sea trench contains the deepest known point in the oceans?
99483.e: In the Challenger Deep of the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific, almost 11,000 m has been measured. No other place in the sea is deeper.
99483.m: The Mariana Trench is the deepest trench on Earth.

99484.q: Which Swiss man reached the bottom of the Mariana Trench together with Don Walsh in 1960?
99484.e: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh dived into the Challenger Deep in the submersible Trieste on 23 January 1960. It was the first visit by people to the deepest point of the sea.
99484.m: In 1960 Jacques Piccard was the first to dive to the deepest point of the sea.

99485.q: Who designed the deep-sea submersible Trieste, with which the Mariana Trench was reached?
99485.e: The Swiss physicist Auguste Piccard developed the principle of the bathyscaphe. The Trieste was built in Italy in 1953 and later taken over by the US Navy.
99485.m: Auguste Piccard built the bathyscaphe Trieste.

99486.q: From what depth does the hadal zone begin, which occurs almost only in deep-sea trenches?
99486.e: The hadal zone is named after the Greek Hades. It includes the deepest areas of the ocean below the abyssal plains.
99486.m: The hadal zone begins at a depth of about 6000 m.

99487.q: Roughly how high is the water pressure at the bottom of the Mariana Trench if it increases by about 1 bar for every 10 m of depth?
99487.e: Almost 11,000 m divided by 10 m gives about 1100 bar. That is over a thousand times more than the air pressure at the sea surface.
99487.m: At the deepest point of the sea the pressure is over 1000 bar.

99488.q: Who was the first person to dive alone to the bottom of the Challenger Deep, in 2012?
99488.e: The film director James Cameron reached the Challenger Deep on 26 March 2012 in the submersible Deepsea Challenger. This made him the first solo diver at this spot.
99488.m: In 2012 James Cameron dived alone into the Mariana Trench.

99490.q: In which deep-sea trench is the deepest point of the Atlantic Ocean?
99490.e: The Puerto Rico Trench reaches a depth of about 8400 m. It lies on the boundary between the Caribbean and North American Plates.
99490.m: The deepest point of the Atlantic is in the Puerto Rico Trench.

99590.q: In the ER model, what is an entity type, for example “pupil” in a school database?
a: A kind of object about which data is stored
A single column of a table
99590.e: An entity type groups objects of the same kind, such as all pupils. In the relational model, it usually becomes a table of its own.
99590.m: An entity type describes a kind of object in a database.

99591.q: Which symbol is used to show a relationship in Chen notation?
99591.e: In Chen notation, rectangles stand for entity types, diamonds for relationships and ellipses for attributes.
99591.m: In Chen notation, a relationship is a diamond.

99592.q: What cardinality does the relationship “pupil attends course” have if each pupil attends several courses and each course has several pupils?
99592.e: Several partners can be involved on both sides. Such a relationship is called n:m or many-to-many.
99592.m: If both sides have several partners, the relationship is n:m.

99593.q: How is an n:m relationship represented when converting to the relational model?
a: By a separate relationship table with two foreign keys
By a foreign key in one of the two tables
99593.e: A relational table can only store one value per column in each row. That is why you need a junction table that contains one key from each side.
99593.m: An n:m relationship becomes a separate junction table.

99594.q: In a 1:n relationship between class and pupil in the relational model, where is the foreign key?
99594.e: Each pupil belongs to exactly one class. That is why you store the key of their class with each pupil.
99594.m: With 1:n, the foreign key is on the n side.

99595.q: What is a weak entity in the ER model?
a: An entity that can only be uniquely identified together with another entity
An entity that is rarely queried
An entity with only one record
99595.e: One example is a room that is only unique together with the building number. In Chen notation it is drawn as a double rectangle.
99595.m: A weak entity needs another entity to be identified.

99596.q: In the ER model, what do you call the properties of an entity type, such as name or date of birth?
99596.e: Attributes describe the features of an entity. In the relational model, they become columns of a table.
99596.m: Attributes describe the properties of an entity.

99597.q: Where does crow's foot notation for ER diagrams get its name from?
a: From the branching line end that marks the many side of a relationship
From the shape of the attribute symbols
99597.e: The three-pronged end of the connecting line looks like a crow's foot. It shows that many entities can be involved on that side.
99597.m: In crow's foot notation, the foot shows the many side.

99598.q: Which two conditions must a primary key in a relational table meet?
a: It must be unique and must not be empty (NULL)
It must be a number and must not be greater than 1000
It must be sorted alphabetically and changeable
It must consist of text and may appear more than once
99598.e: A primary key identifies every row. That is why no value may appear twice and no value may be missing.
99598.m: A primary key is unique and never empty.

99599.q: What do you call a primary key made up of several columns together?
99599.e: Sometimes only the combination of several columns is unique, for example course number and pupil number in a junction table.
99599.m: A composite key consists of several columns.

a: An artificial key with no business meaning, such as a running number
A key formed from the name
A key that refers to another table
A key that only applies temporarily
99600.e: Surrogate keys are assigned by the system, for example with AUTO_INCREMENT. They never change, even if the business data changes.
99600.m: A surrogate key is an artificial number with no meaning.

99601.q: What do you call all the minimal column combinations that could serve as the primary key?
99601.e: From the candidate keys you choose one as the primary key. The others are called alternate keys.
99601.m: Candidate keys are all the possible primary keys.

99602.q: Why is a person's name usually not a good primary key?
a: Because several people can have the same name
Because names must not contain letters
99602.e: Names are not unique and can also change, for example on marriage. But a primary key must identify every row uniquely and permanently.
99602.m: Names are not suitable as primary keys because they are not unique.

99603.q: How many digits does the Swiss AHV number (social security number), used as a unique personal number, have?
99603.e: The AHV number (AHVN13) has 13 digits and begins with the country code 756. It is an example of a natural key.
99603.m: The Swiss AHV number consists of 13 digits.

99604.q: Which data structure does a database system usually create automatically for a primary key so that it can search quickly?
a: An index, usually as a B-tree
99604.e: A B-tree index makes it possible to find a key in logarithmic time. At the same time, it checks uniqueness efficiently.
99604.m: A B-tree index is usually created for the primary key.

99605.q: What is the maximum number of primary keys a relational table can have?
a: Exactly one, which can consist of several columns
99605.e: A table has exactly one primary key. You can mark further unique columns with UNIQUE as alternate keys.
99605.m: Every table has exactly one primary key.

a: Every foreign key value refers to an existing record
All tables have the same number of rows
99606.e: The database system prevents references to nothing. A foreign key may only contain values that occur in the referenced table, or NULL.
99606.m: Referential integrity prevents references to records that do not exist.

99607.q: What does the option ON DELETE CASCADE do for a foreign key?
a: Dependent records are deleted too when the referenced record is deleted
The foreign key is set to zero
99607.e: If a customer is deleted, for example, CASCADE also deletes their orders. With SET NULL, the reference would be emptied instead.
99607.m: ON DELETE CASCADE automatically deletes dependent records as well.

99608.q: May a foreign key column contain the value NULL?
a: Yes, if the relationship is optional
Only if the table is empty
99608.e: NULL means that there is no reference, for example for an employee without a department. If you want to prevent this, you also set NOT NULL.
99608.m: A foreign key may be NULL if the relationship is optional.

99609.q: In an “Employee” table, how do you model that every employee has a manager who is also an employee?
a: With a foreign key that refers to the same table
With a composite primary key of name and salary
With a column of type BLOB
99609.e: A self-referencing foreign key, such as manager_id, refers to the id of another row in the same table. This creates hierarchies.
99609.m: A foreign key can also refer to its own table.

99610.q: Which columns may a foreign key refer to in SQL?
a: A primary key or a unique column
Only columns in the same table
99610.e: The referenced value must be unique so that it is clear which record is meant. That is why you refer to a PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE column.
99610.m: A foreign key refers to a unique column.

99611.q: Which SQL operation typically links two tables through foreign key and primary key?
99611.e: With a JOIN, rows are combined whose foreign key matches the primary key of the other table, for example ON o.customer_id = c.id.
99611.m: With a JOIN, you link tables through their keys.
